before: Constructive conditions are commonly associated in the school model with relatively low, less steep waves and sufficient time for swash to move material onto the beach. Weaker returning transport can leave sediment behind. Destructive conditions are commonly associated with higher, steeper waves and stronger backwash relative to swash, removing material from parts of the beach and potentially storing it farther offshore. Real beach response also depends on wave period, breaking form, beach slope, permeability, sediment size and the sequence of events. A single label does not replace these controls.
after: Constructive waves are low-energy waves. They are low, with a long wavelength, and break infrequently, so the swash of one wave has time to soak away before the next arrives. They spill gently onto the beach, giving a strong swash and a weak backwash, so sand and pebbles are carried up the beach and left there. Destructive waves are high-energy waves, often driven by strong winds during storms. They are high and steep, with a short wavelength, and break frequently. They plunge down onto the beach, so the swash is weak and the backwash strong: material is dragged down the beach and may be stored offshore in a bar. Beach slope, sediment size and the sequence of events also affect the result.

after.prompt: Distinguish constructive and destructive waves by their energy, form and effect on the beach.

before: Longshore drift is the net transport of beach material along the coast through oblique swash and returning backwash. Waves approaching at an angle can send swash diagonally up the beach. Gravity then returns backwash more directly downslope. Repeated movements give sediment a zigzag path with a net alongshore component. The direction depends on wave approach and the orientation of the shore; it is not invariably north, south or to the right of a page. Longshore currents can also transport sediment within the nearshore system.

before: A beach is an accumulation of loose material such as sand, shingle or pebbles along the shore. Waves and currents sort and redistribute the sediment, producing a changing profile. Beaches can include different zones and seasonal forms. Their material may come from rivers, cliff erosion, offshore deposits or transport from elsewhere along the coast. A beach should not be defined as sand alone or assumed to be permanently the same width. Tidal level and the reference line used for measurement affect the visible exposed width on a particular date.
after: A beach is an accumulation of loose material such as sand, shingle or pebbles along the shore. Waves and currents sort and redistribute the sediment, producing a changing profile. Material is often sorted by size across the beach. Strong swash, especially from storm waves, throws large pebbles to the back of the beach, while the weaker backwash can carry only smaller material back down. Material near the water is moved most often, so attrition makes it smaller and rounder. Large pebbles are therefore often found at the top of the beach and finer material nearer the sea. before: Headlands are projections of land into the sea, while bays are coastal indentations between or beside them. In a simple differential-erosion model, less resistant rock is removed more rapidly, creating bays, while more resistant rock remains as headlands. A bay may have a depositional beach within it, so its existence does not imply that every part is undergoing rapid erosion at the time observed.

before: Convection and plate movement form a connected system. Rising and spreading mantle flow can be associated with plates moving apart, while colder oceanic lithosphere can descend at a subduction zone. The sinking slab helps pull the rest of its plate, and the elevated position of a ridge also contributes to motion away from it. A school convection sketch simplifies these relationships. It should not imply that friction from one circular current is the sole force moving every plate or that all currents have identical sizes.
after: Convection currents move the plates. Where a current rises beneath the lithosphere, it spreads out sideways in two directions. The sideways-moving mantle drags the plate above it, like a slow conveyor belt. Plates therefore move apart above a rising current, as at a mid-ocean ridge, where magma rises into the gap. Where two currents meet and sink, the plates above them are dragged towards each other, as at a destructive margin. Scientists now think that two further forces also help: the cold, dense oceanic plate sinking at a subduction zone pulls the rest of its plate (slab pull), and the raised ridge pushes plates away from it (ridge push).

before.prompt: Describe the sequence of mantle convection associated with plate movement.
before.canonical_answer: Hotter, less dense mantle material rises slowly. It spreads and transfers heat nearer the lithosphere. Cooler, denser material sinks elsewhere, completing circulation connected to plate motion.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first upward step and its density relationship; 1 for spreading and heat transfer; 1 for sinking as the result of cooling/density change. Do not require a claim that the whole mantle is liquid.

after.prompt: Describe how convection currents in the mantle cause plates to move.
after.canonical_answer: Heat from the interior makes mantle material hotter and less dense, so it rises slowly. Beneath the lithosphere it spreads sideways and drags the plates above it. Plates move apart above the rising current and are dragged towards each other where cooled, denser material sinks.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for heated, less dense material rising; 1 for sideways flow beneath the lithosphere dragging the overlying plate; 1 for plates moving apart above rising flow and together where cooled material sinks. Do not require a claim that the whole mantle is liquid.

before.canonical_answer: The A–B–C sequence shows upward flow followed by sideways spreading and downward return. The surface plates diverge above A. The flow pattern is consistent with convection associated with a constructive setting.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the rising-to-sideways flow pattern; 1 for the cooler downward return shown by the data; 1 for relating the apart-pointing surface arrows to divergence.

after.canonical_answer: The A–B–C sequence shows upward flow, sideways spreading and downward return of cooler material. The sideways flow at B drags the plates above it in opposite directions, so the surface plates diverge above A. This is the convection pattern found beneath a constructive margin.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the rising-to-sideways flow pattern; 1 for the cooler downward return shown by the data; 1 for linking the sideways flow dragging the plates to the apart-pointing surface arrows (divergence).

before.prompt: How far do you agree that the cheapest initial gabion proposal is necessarily best over ten years? The exposed site has damaged baskets nearby and the proposal includes no repair funding. Judge sustained protection within total costs.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with necessity. Low initial cost omits likely maintenance needs suggested by the damaged-basket evidence. Exposure and unfunded repair could undermine performance, so lifetime cost and suitability need assessment before the proposal can be preferred.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging initial versus lifetime cost, condition/exposure evidence and the maintenance consequence.
1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting price alone as sufficient.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that gabions are a suitable defence for this frontage? A 60 m dune edge beside a car park is being cut back by moderate waves; the site is fairly sheltered, the budget is small, and the council will inspect and repair the defence every year. Judge protection, cost and durability. [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Gabions are cheap and quick to build, and their rock-filled baskets absorb some wave energy, which suits a short frontage with moderate waves and a small budget. Yearly inspection deals with their main weakness. However, the wire baskets can rust or break in storms and salt spray, so they are a short- to medium-term defence that needs repairs, and they protect only the edge directly behind them. Overall they are suitable here because exposure is moderate and maintenance is funded, but they would be a poor choice on a stormy, unmaintained coast.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for weighing low cost and energy absorption on a short, moderately exposed frontage against wire damage, limited lifespan and local-only protection, using the supplied site conditions.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision that links suitability to the moderate exposure and funded maintenance.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that one beach-nourishment programme is sufficient to maintain width without further spending? Suitable sand is added, but waves redistribute it and the plan has no future supply or monitoring budget. Judge sustained width.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree. Nourishment adds sediment and can widen the beach, but redistribution is part of the system. Without monitoring or provision for repeat supply, sustained width is uncertain. Sand movement alone does not prove failure, but sustained width is not established.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for the sediment-input benefit, redistribution evidence and repeat-funding/monitoring limitation.
1 C mark for a supported judgement rejecting the guarantee while retaining the benefit.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that beach nourishment is the best way to keep this tourist beach wide? The town’s main beach is narrowing by about 2 m a year, suitable sand is available offshore, and the council can pay for a refill every few years but cannot afford a seawall. Judge sustained width and cost. [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Nourishment adds sand directly, so it widens the beach and keeps a natural sandy surface that tourists use, and a seawall is both unaffordable and unable to rebuild beach width. Suitable sand and funded refills make it workable. However, waves and currents keep moving the added sand, so the beach will narrow again and refills must continue and be monitored; a run of storms or a funding cut would stop it working. Groynes could help hold the sand longer. Overall nourishment is the best option here, provided refills and monitoring continue.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for weighing direct sand input, a natural recreational beach and affordability against redistribution, the need for repeated refills and monitoring, and dependence on funding or storm conditions.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision that states the condition on which nourishment succeeds.

before: HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks the immune system. AIDS is acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, associated with the most advanced stage of HIV infection. HIV names the virus; AIDS names a syndrome, not a different virus. A person living with HIV should not automatically be described as having AIDS. Effective treatment can support a long, healthy life, so diagnosis is not a prediction of an inevitable immediate outcome.
after: HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks the immune system. AIDS is acquired immunodeficiency syndrome: the most advanced stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is so weakened that the body can no longer fight illnesses such as tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections. HIV names the virus; AIDS names the syndrome, not a different virus. A person living with HIV does not necessarily have AIDS, and effective treatment can stop AIDS from developing.

before: The named examples show spatial variation, with the north-eastern and north-central examples higher than the two lower examples in this historical record. Explaining the pattern requires evidence about factors such as prevention access, treatment and survival, population composition, mobility and unequal exposure. A regional comparison alone cannot establish the cause or justify stereotyping its residents.
after: The pattern can be explained. In 2017 national adult prevalence was 12.6%, so Zambezi and Ohangwena were well above the national figure and Kunene and Khomas below it. Zambezi is almost surrounded by Zambia, Botswana and Angola. The Trans-Caprivi Highway carries trucks through Katima Mulilo into Zambia as part of the Walvis Bay Corridor. Truck drivers, migrant workers and traders spend long periods away from home, which increases the chance of several sexual partners and spreads the virus along routes and in border towns.

before: Prevalence can reflect both new infections and survival. Comparing regions also requires compatible methods and age groups. Overlapping uncertainty intervals limit simple ranking claims, while a national average conceals local variation. Use newer compatible estimates for a current decision; this dated survey remains useful for practising interpretation without presenting an old spatial pattern as permanently unchanged.
after: Ohangwena borders Angola and is densely settled, with about 32 people per km² in 2023, so cross-border movement and contact between many people help the virus spread. Kunene had only about one person per km², so fewer contacts and less movement help explain its lower prevalence. Women's lower social and economic status can increase their risk in every region. Prevalence also reflects survival on treatment, so a regional figure shows both new infections and how long people live with HIV.

before: An enterprise's absence record needs interpretation. Fewer days missed after improved care may be consistent with better health support, but seasonal work, staffing or reporting changes could also matter. A person's private status should not be inferred from attendance. Use appropriately protected aggregate records and relevant context, distinguishing an observed association from an isolated medical cause.
after: At national level the effects were large before treatment was widely available. United States Census Bureau estimates for 2008 put Namibia's life expectancy at about 50 years, compared with about 71 years in a model without AIDS, and the crude death rate at 14 per 1,000 instead of 5. Population growth was about 0.9% a year instead of 1.9%. WHO estimated that about 57,000 children had lost one or both parents to AIDS by the end of 2003.

before: Demographic and economic records also need compatible timeframes. A treatment programme may improve survival before a measurable change appears in labour-market or population indicators. A single year's earnings can change for reasons beyond health. Compare suitable records over time, retain uncertainty and identify the level of the claim: person, household, enterprise or country. Evidence at one level does not automatically establish an equal effect at all others.
after: Most AIDS deaths occur among adults aged about 15 to 49, the economically active and child-bearing ages. On a population pyramid the bars for these ages become narrower. Social impacts are effects on people, families and communities: more orphans and child-headed households, grandparents caring for grandchildren, children leaving school to nurse sick relatives or earn money, and stigma that isolates families.

before: A supported conclusion recognises both potential impacts and effective responses. It can explain how preventable illness or discrimination creates pressure while acknowledging that treatment and supportive conditions allow people to lead productive lives. This balance is essential for accurate population analysis and avoids turning an economic discussion into a stereotype about people living with HIV.
after: Economic impacts concern money, work and production. Illness and deaths reduce the number of skilled and experienced workers, so firms lose productivity and must recruit and train replacements. Absenteeism rises, household incomes and savings fall, and fewer people pay tax. Government spends more on health care, medicines and grants, leaving less for other development. Treatment reduces many of these effects by keeping people healthy enough to work.

before: Namibian health authorities and partners have undertaken surveillance and treatment-response work, including NAMPHIA's dated household survey and linked information for services. The survey provides evidence about a period; it is not proof that every current target has been met. A current response judgement needs appropriate recent service and outcome records, with the same care about dates and groups used for population statistics.
after: In Namibia the government leads the response through the Ministry of Health and Social Services. It launched the national antiretroviral programme in government health facilities in 2003, and ART is provided free of charge in the public sector. It also runs programmes to prevent mother-to-child transmission (begun in 2002), voluntary counselling and testing, free condom distribution and awareness campaigns, especially for women and young people. The National Code on HIV/AIDS and Employment forbids discrimination at work because of a person's HIV status.

before: A training programme illustrates the activity/outcome distinction. Suppose fifty workers attend a session about confidential referrals. Attendance establishes that the session occurred and those workers participated. Later evidence is needed to show accurate referrals, respectful practice or improved access. A good evaluation identifies that missing link and proposes suitable follow-up rather than treating a certificate count as a completed health outcome.
after: Regional and local authorities take part in the committees that plan the response in each area. They can include HIV awareness in their town services and support clinics and community programmes. Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) offer counselling and testing, home-based care for sick people, food and emotional support for people on treatment, and help for orphans and vulnerable children. NGOs reach remote villages through volunteers, but many depend on donor funding that can end.

before: Programme evaluation also needs fairness and privacy. A high national coverage figure can conceal lower access for some locations or groups. Relevant disaggregation can identify barriers, but small samples require careful interpretation and protection of identities. A region's average should not be assigned to a particular person, and people should not be required to reveal status for a school exercise.
after: Churches and faith-based organisations reach many people because about 90% of Namibians are Christian. They provide counselling, home visits and care for the sick, help orphans with food, school fees and uniforms, and use their meetings to reduce stigma and encourage testing. Some faith-based institutions also provide treatment. A weakness is that some religious messages discourage condom use or present HIV as a moral failing, which can increase stigma.

before: Sustainable delivery needs finance, staff and supply continuity. A temporary campaign can improve awareness while long-term care remains dependent on maintained services. Monitoring should distinguish the immediate reach from continued usable access. A supported judgement can recognise real progress while explaining the remaining constraint, without claiming success or failure solely from money spent, people attending or a target announced.
after: Private firms can run workplace programmes with testing, condoms and education, keep employees' status confidential and allow time off for treatment; a national business coalition on HIV/AIDS was set up in 2004 to support this work. Individuals can get tested and know their status, use condoms correctly, reduce their number of sexual partners, take treatment every day if they are positive, and support people living with HIV instead of excluding them.

before: A prevention campaign can distribute condoms or provide information, but observed protection depends on access and actual correct consistent use. Distribution is an input measure. It does not establish a specific fall in infections or pregnancies without relevant evidence. The geographical question concerns how an effective measure connects to demographic outcomes, rather than a claim that handing out a product automatically changes a national rate.
after: Correct and consistent condom use affects population structure in two ways. First, fewer unplanned pregnancies lower the birth rate, so the base of the population pyramid becomes narrower and population growth slows. Second, fewer HIV infections mean fewer adults aged about 15 to 49 fall ill and die, so the working-age bars stay wide, fewer children become orphans and more people survive into old age. These effects depend on people actually using condoms.

before: A hypothetical programme record shows attendance improving after sustained usable care, with employment conditions and recording otherwise stated comparable. That is consistent with preserved participation. Without a suitable comparison, it does not isolate the exact contribution of treatment from every other change. A careful answer explains the mechanism and the evidence limit instead of promising a fixed national productivity gain.
after: Wider use of ARVs mainly lowers the death rate. Fewer adults die young, so the middle bars of the pyramid stay wide, life expectancy rises and more people reach the older age groups, widening the top of the pyramid. Fewer children lose their parents. Because deaths fall while births continue, population growth can speed up slightly, adding to future demand for schools, jobs and housing.

before: Population structure changes over time. Preventing premature adult deaths can preserve cohorts and caregivers, while reducing new infections can protect future health. Effects on an age pyramid depend on the original structure, births and movement as well as survival. One programme total cannot provide the complete future pyramid. A supported conclusion names the component affected and avoids claiming that treatment or condoms must increase or decrease the whole population in every setting.
after: ARVs also affect the economy. Workers stay healthy enough to keep their jobs, so skills and experience are kept, absenteeism falls and households keep their income. Fewer orphans and sick relatives reduce the cost of care for families and the state. However, treatment is a large, lifelong cost: the government must buy medicines, pay health workers and run clinics, using money that could otherwise go to education or roads.

before: Environmental effects can extend beyond immediate destruction. Ash and lava alter land surfaces and habitats; polluted or blocked waterways affect ecosystems; landslides and tsunami deposits reshape landscapes. Some volcanic soils can become productive after weathering over time, and volcanic areas may support geothermal energy and tourism. These longer-term opportunities do not cancel immediate hazards or imply that fresh ash is automatically fertile and safe. A judgement should specify its time period, location and affected group. A farmer losing a crop during an eruption faces a different issue from later agricultural use of weathered material.
after: Environmental effects can extend beyond immediate destruction. Ash and lava alter land surfaces and habitats; polluted or blocked waterways affect ecosystems; landslides and tsunami deposits reshape landscapes. Even so, many people choose to live near volcanoes and active faults. Volcanic material weathers over time into very fertile farming soils. Volcanic areas offer geothermal energy, hot springs and scenery that attract tourists, and some old volcanic rocks contain valuable minerals. Other reasons are social and economic: people have jobs, land and family in the area, cannot afford to move or have nowhere else to go. Large eruptions and earthquakes may be many years apart, so people may judge the risk to be small or trust warnings and strong buildings. These benefits come later: fresh ash still destroys the crops of the year in which it falls.

before: These processes connect with settlement location, water resources and research skills. A hazard is the potentially damaging physical event; disaster risk also reflects exposure and vulnerability. The same earthquake can have different consequences in two places with different buildings, ground conditions and response capacity. Observations about damaged structures should therefore not be used to infer the Earth’s internal state without further evidence. Equally, knowing the plate setting does not establish that every house will collapse. Physical explanation and evidence about the community are both necessary for a supported account of risk.
after: These processes connect with settlement location, water resources and research skills. A hazard is the potentially damaging physical event; disaster risk also reflects exposure and vulnerability. An earthquake of the same magnitude usually kills more people in a low-income country (LEDC) than in a high-income country (MEDC). Most deaths are caused by buildings collapsing, and in poorer countries more buildings are made of weak materials and building codes are often not enforced. Warning systems, drills, rescue teams, hospitals and equipment may be limited, and poor roads slow the arrival of help. Wealthier countries can afford earthquake-resistant buildings and trained emergency services, although a very large event can still overwhelm them, as in Japan in 2011. The depth of the focus, distance from the epicentre, population density, time of day and ground conditions also affect the death toll.

before.canonical_answer: Lava.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the name lava.

after.prompt: Name one benefit that attracts people to live near a volcano despite the risk of eruption.
after.canonical_answer: Fertile soils formed from weathered volcanic material. Geothermal energy, tourism or minerals are also acceptable.

before.prompt:
(a) Name the surface point vertically above an earthquake’s focus. [1]
(b) Describe three stages connecting a locked fault to earthquake shaking. [3]
(c) Name the Earth’s central metallic layer. [1]
(d) Describe two observations in this record that support an internal-layer distinction: R is a thin solid outer rock layer, while T is metallic and central. [2]
before.canonical_answer: (a) Epicentre. (b) Stress builds during locking; sudden slip releases stored energy; seismic waves produce shaking. (c) Core. (d) R is an outer rocky layer whereas T is central; their rock-versus-metal composition also differs.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for epicentre.
(b) 3 A marks: stress while locked, sudden slip/energy release, seismic-wave shaking; credit distinct stages.
(c) 1 A mark for core.
(d) 2 B marks for two interpreted resource contrasts: outer/central position and rock/metal material. No double credit for repeating the same point.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that hazard information alone is sufficient to protect a community? A weak school remains occupied; officials provide warnings, but no strengthening, transport or shelter is funded. Judge protection against collapse and effective evacuation.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree substantially. Warnings can alert people and support decisions, but cannot strengthen the weak school. Without transport, some residents may be unable to leave; without shelter, evacuation may not be sustainable. Information is useful, but structural protection and practical evacuation support are also needed for the specified dangers.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 marks for judgement of the given evidence: distinguish warning value from unchanged collapse risk; analyse transport and shelter limitations and their consequences. Do not credit unsupported general lists.
1 mark for a supported overall decision addressing sufficiency against the stated criterion; an implied but clear conclusion is acceptable.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that an earthquake of a given magnitude will always cause more deaths in a low-income country than in a high-income country? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Most deaths happen when buildings collapse, and low-income countries more often have weak buildings, unenforced building codes, few warning systems or drills, and limited rescue teams, hospitals and roads, so more people are killed or die before help arrives. However, "always" goes too far. The death toll also depends on the depth of the focus, the distance from the epicentre, population density, the time of day and the ground. A shallow earthquake beneath a crowded city in a rich country can kill more people than a deep one under a thinly populated area of a poorer country, and a very large event, such as the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami in Japan, can overwhelm strong preparation. Overall, wealth makes a large difference to the death toll, but it is not the only factor.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that making buildings earthquake-resistant is the most effective way to reduce deaths from earthquakes? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Most earthquake deaths are caused by collapsing buildings, so building to earthquake-resistant standards, enforcing building codes and strengthening existing schools and hospitals tackle the main cause directly. after.prompt: How far do you agree that monitoring a volcano is the most important way to reduce deaths from an eruption? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. However, monitoring cannot say exactly when an eruption will happen, how large it will be or which way flows will travel, and on its own it saves no lives. People must receive and trust the warnings, and there must be transport, safe routes and shelter so that they can leave and stay away. Hazard maps that keep homes out of valleys where lava, pyroclastic flows and lahars travel also reduce deaths. Monitoring is an essential first step, but evacuation planning and land-use control are just as important.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that providing free antiretroviral treatment is the most important effort the Namibian government makes against HIV and AIDS?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Free ART in public facilities since 2003 keeps people living with HIV alive and able to work, cuts AIDS deaths among 15 to 49 year olds and means fewer children are orphaned. People on effective treatment do not pass HIV on sexually, so treatment also prevents new infections. However, ART alone does not stop people becoming infected: free condoms, testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission and awareness campaigns are needed to reduce new cases, and treatment is a large lifelong cost. Overall ART is the most important single effort for saving lives, but it works best combined with prevention.

after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Prevention through free condoms, testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission and education for young people reduces new infections, so fewer people need lifelong treatment later, and preventing an infection costs less than treating it. However, treatment keeps many people alive and working, protects children from becoming orphans, and itself prevents sexual transmission when the virus is suppressed, so cutting it would raise deaths and new infections. Prevention deserves more attention, but both must be funded together.

Local authorities provide permanent town services and land, include HIV in local planning and take part in the regional committees that coordinate the response. How far do you agree that Zambezi had the highest prevalence of these regions mainly because of its transport routes and borders? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Zambezi is almost surrounded by Zambia, Botswana and Angola, and the Trans-Caprivi Highway carries trucks through Katima Mulilo into Zambia. Truck drivers, migrant workers and traders spend long periods away from home and may have several partners, spreading HIV along the route and in border towns. Ohangwena, also high, borders Angola and is densely settled, while thinly populated Kunene is low, which supports the movement explanation. However, other factors matter: women's lower social and economic status raises their risk, and prevalence also reflects how long people survive on treatment. Zambezi's estimate also has a wide uncertainty range (17.5 to 27.0%). Mobility is the main explanation, but not the only one.

before: A testable hypothesis might predict that environmental quality is lower at heavily used visitor sites than at comparable quieter sites. Select sites using a clear sampling design. Random selection gives eligible sites a chance of selection; systematic selection uses a regular rule; stratified selection represents defined groups such as busy and quiet zones. Record the chosen approach, coverage and limitations rather than claiming that any one design removes all bias.
after: The usual recording sheet is a bi-polar grid. Each row pairs a positive description with its opposite, such as “no litter” and “litter everywhere”, with a scale between them, for example +2, +1, 0, −1, −2. Choose rows that suit the hypothesis: litter, noise, trampled vegetation, congestion, condition of facilities. Put every positive description on the same side so that the row scores can be added into a site total.

before: Observers should calibrate category meanings on a practice site, then record scores and relevant notes independently. Use a safe location and avoid disturbing people or wildlife. Repeated visits at matched times improve comparisons. A one-day assessment describes the sampled conditions, while seasonal conclusions need observations across seasons.
after: Use enough sites to show a pattern: two sites cannot show a trend, so five or more, for example at set distances from a viewpoint or campsite, give more meaningful results. Survey every site at the same time of day, because noise, traffic and litter change through the day. Observers should first practise on one site so that they read the descriptions the same way, then score independently.

before: Suppose three indicators each use 0 for poor, 1 for intermediate and 2 for good. A site scoring 1,0,2 has a total of three out of six. Higher totals represent better assessed quality under that scheme. Compare the totals and individual indicators, looking for exceptions. Subjectivity, changing collection schedules and weather may affect the result; repeated matched observations and clearer scoring anchors can improve reliability.
after: Suppose a grid has five rows scored +2 to −2, so a site total can range from −10 to +10. A site beside a car park scores −1, −2, 0, −1, +1, a total of −3. A site 500 m away scores +2, +1, +1, +2, +1, a total of +7, showing better assessed quality. A simpler sheet scores each indicator 0 (poor), 1 or 2 (good); its totals are compared in the same way.

before: For a paired teaching dataset, visitor counts of 10, 30 and 50 accompany quality totals of 6, 4 and 2. The inverse relationship supports lower assessed quality at busier sites. If the facilities indicator remains 2 at all three, the separate hypothesis of declining facilities scores is unsupported despite the falling totals.
after: Present the totals as a bar chart, or plot each site total against distance or visitor count. A profile graph of one site's row scores shows which indicators are poor. If totals of 6, 4 and 2 match visitor counts of 10, 30 and 50 while the facilities score stays at 2, quality falls with use but facilities did not decline.

before: A testable hypothesis might predict greater path width at sites with higher pedestrian counts during matched observation periods. Select sites by a recorded random, systematic or stratified design, using the chosen rule consistently. Measure repeated widths at each site, record units and calculate a mean. Count passers-by over the same duration and time window. A width measured over years and a ten-minute count describe different timescales, so association does not prove present users caused the entire path form.
after: A common investigation tests whether footpath erosion decreases with distance from a tourist hot spot such as a car park, viewpoint or lodge. Most visitors walk the first stretch of path, so trampling is concentrated there. Use systematic sampling: place measurement stations at regular intervals, for example every 20 m, along the path away from the hot spot. Regular spacing covers the whole path and avoids choosing only the worst-eroded places.

before: Record slope, surface material, rainfall history and maintenance where relevant. These can influence erosion independently of visitor pressure. Compare matched sites or account for those differences when interpreting results. A wider path may reflect deliberate construction rather than erosion, which is why the operational definition and contextual observations matter.
after: At each station, measure width between the edges of bare ground with a tape held at right angles to the path. For depth, lay a ranging pole across the path and measure down to the surface with a ruler at five equally spaced points, then take the mean. Record slope, surface material and drainage, because steep or wet sections can erode faster whatever the number of walkers.

before: Plot the supplied paired values on provided axes using the stated units and scale. Describe the overall relationship and any exception, then decide which hypothesis the evidence supports. Repeated measurements reduce random reading error but do not remove biased site selection. Additional seasons, comparable sites and clearer edge definitions improve different parts of the design. Each proposed improvement should name the limitation it addresses.
after: Plot distance on the horizontal axis and mean width or depth on the vertical axis. Describe the overall trend, then identify any anomaly and suggest a reason, such as a steep or waterlogged section. Pedestrian counts at each station over the same period test whether use also falls with distance, although a short count shows present use, not the years of use that formed the path.

before: A teaching record gives mean widths of 110, 150 and 130 cm at sites with 20, 40 and 60 passers-by. Width does not increase at every step: the third site is narrower than the second. Depths of 1, 2 and 3 cm show a different pattern. Judge each measured feature separately.
after: For example, mean widths of 240, 180, 130, 150 and 90 cm at 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 m show a general decrease away from the hot spot, with an anomaly at 60 m that needs a site explanation. Width and depth can show different patterns, so judge each measured feature separately.

before: Random selection uses a chance rule within a defined eligible group; systematic selection follows a rule such as every fifth eligible person after a suitable start; stratified selection covers defined groups, with a clear rule within each. Non-response should be recorded rather than replaced silently with convenient respondents. Surveying only near one attraction or at one hour can omit important groups.
after: Random selection uses a chance rule within a defined group; systematic selection follows a rule such as every fifth person passing; stratified selection makes sure groups such as residents, visitors and business owners are all included. Record people who decline instead of replacing them silently with convenient respondents.

before: Seasonal comparisons require observations from the seasons being compared. Asking people to remember a previous season provides perceptions or recalled information, with possible recall error; it is different from direct matched counts. Record the question, sample size, timing and location so percentages have a clear denominator. Twelve positive answers among twenty respondents is 60% of that sample, not proof that 60% of every resident agrees.
after: Closed questions offer fixed answers, such as yes/no, tick boxes or a 1–5 rating scale; they are quick to answer and easy to tally and graph. Open questions, such as “Why did you visit?”, give detail but are harder to group. Keep wording short and neutral: “Has tourism changed your household income?”, not “Tourism has helped you, hasn't it?”. A pilot survey with a few people shows which questions confuse. Remembered answers about a past season are perceptions, not direct counts.

before: Link conclusions to the evidence and sampling limits. A larger sample can improve coverage but does not by itself correct leading wording or exclusion of non-users. Better time coverage, neutral wording and a suitable selection rule address different problems. Combine survey findings with relevant observed conditions or business records when the claim concerns measured seasonality rather than opinion alone.
after: Business surveys judge tourism's economic and seasonal impact. Ask owners or managers of lodges, shops, craft stalls and tour operators which months are busiest, whether they employ extra staff in the busy season, roughly what share of customers are tourists, and where most supplies are bought: locally, elsewhere in Namibia or imported. Busy and quiet season answers show changes in income and jobs; the supplies question shows leakage.

before: A matched survey example records 12 positive answers among 20 residents in a quiet period and eight among 20 in a busy period. The positive shares are 60% and 40%. If observed visitor counts rise from 20 to 60, greater use is supported while greater positive resident response is not.
after: State the sample size with every result: twelve “yes” answers from 20 residents is 60% of that sample, not of all residents. Use a pie chart or divided bar for shares in each category, and side-by-side bars to compare a quiet and a busy season.

before.prompt: Explain why observers should practise using the same environmental-quality scoring anchors before comparing sites.
before.canonical_answer: Different personal interpretations can give different scores for the same condition. Shared practice and clearer anchors reduce that inconsistency, improving comparability without removing all judgement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the subjectivity reason; 1 for the comparability improvement because shared anchors reduce disagreement.

after.prompt: Explain why a bi-polar environmental-quality grid keeps the positive description on the same side in every row.
after.canonical_answer: Then a high score always means better conditions in every row, so the row scores can be added into a site total and the totals of different sites compared fairly.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the consistent meaning of the scores across rows.
1 mark for explaining that this allows totals to be added and sites compared.

before.prompt: Explain why one ten-minute pedestrian count cannot establish that present users caused the entire measured path width.
before.canonical_answer: Width reflects a longer history and can also depend on construction, slope, surface or maintenance. The short count can show current use, but the timing and alternative factors limit causal attribution.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the timescale/alternative-factor reason; 1 for explaining why association differs from isolated causation.

after.prompt: Explain why measurement stations in a footpath-erosion survey are placed at regular intervals, such as every 20 m, along the path away from a car park.
after.canonical_answer: Systematic spacing covers the whole path evenly, so the investigator cannot choose only badly eroded places (less bias). It also lets width or depth be plotted against distance from the car park to test whether erosion decreases away from it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for even coverage / avoiding biased choice of sites.
1 mark for allowing change in erosion with distance from the hot spot to be shown.

before.prompt: Explain why questioning only visitors cannot establish residents’ views about tourism’s effects.
before.canonical_answer: The sampled population is visitors, while the claim concerns residents. A suitably selected resident sample is needed because the groups can experience different costs and benefits.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the population-mismatch reason; 1 for explaining the relevant resident-evidence remedy.

after.prompt: Explain why a survey of the seasonal economic impact of tourism should include business owners as well as residents.
after.canonical_answer: Business owners can report how customer numbers, takings and staff numbers change between busy and quiet months. Residents' opinions alone cannot measure business income or seasonal jobs.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for what business owners can report (customers, income, staff by season).
1 mark for explaining why resident views alone are insufficient.

after.text: Weathering landforms include scree (talus), angular fragments loosened mainly by freeze-thaw that collect at the foot of a cliff; exfoliation domes, rounded bare-rock hills shedding curved sheets; tors, jointed blocks left where weathering acted along joints; and limestone joints and bedding planes widened by carbonation into grooves and caves.

before: Weathering products can accumulate below an outcrop as loose angular material or remain within a weathered profile. The material may later be moved by gravity, runoff, rivers or wind. Bare rock, fractured blocks, rounded residual masses and solution features all need a process explanation appropriate to their evidence. A landform records a history that may include more than one process and a long period of change. Its present appearance does not establish that every process is active at the same rate today. Distinguish a description of shape from an explanation of development.
after: Weathering produces several landforms. Scree (talus) is a sloping heap of angular rock fragments at the foot of a steep cliff. Freeze-thaw in the joints of the cliff loosens the fragments, which then fall and roll downslope under gravity. An exfoliation dome is a rounded hill of bare rock, often granite, from which curved outer sheets peel away like the layers of an onion; the loose sheets and broken pieces collect at its foot. A tor is a pile of jointed, rounded blocks on a hilltop, left where weathering attacked the rock most strongly along its joints and the loosened material was later removed. In limestone, carbonation widens joints and bedding planes into grooves and, over a very long time, into caves. A landform can record more than one process, so describe its shape first and then explain how it formed.

before: Exfoliation is the detachment of outer rock sheets or layers, often giving an exposed surface a rounded or peeling appearance. Thermal stresses can contribute where surface heating and cooling create differences in expansion and contraction between outer material and the interior. Repeated stresses may help fractures grow and sheets separate. The account concerns changes in the rock’s stress and shape, rather than chemical conversion of the whole block into a new mineral.
after: Exfoliation is the detachment of outer rock sheets or layers, often giving an exposed surface a rounded or peeling appearance. Thermal stresses can contribute where surface heating and cooling create differences in expansion and contraction between outer material and the interior. Repeated stresses may help fractures grow and sheets separate. The account concerns changes in the rock’s stress and shape, rather than chemical conversion of the whole block into a new mineral. Repeated peeling rounds the outcrop into an exfoliation dome, and the fallen sheets and fragments collect as scree at its foot.

before.prompt: Describe the weathering evidence in a specimen that has split into smaller pieces but retains the same mineral composition; the fragments remain beside the original block.
before.canonical_answer: The smaller pieces show physical breakdown. Unchanged minerals support a mechanical rather than chemical interpretation. Retained fragments show in-place change without evidence of removal.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the fragmentation feature; 1 for using the unchanged-mineral evidence; 1 for the retained-fragment evidence and its in-place interpretation.

after.prompt: A field record shows a steep, jointed rock cliff in a mountain area where night temperatures often fall below 0 °C and meltwater enters the joints by day. At the foot of the cliff lies a sloping heap of angular rock fragments. Describe the landform at the foot of the cliff and how weathering produced it, using the record.
after.canonical_answer: The sloping heap of angular fragments is scree (talus). Water in the joints freezes and expands at night and thaws by day, so repeated freeze-thaw widens the joints and loosens angular pieces. The loosened pieces fall and roll down the cliff under gravity and pile up at its foot.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the feature as scree/talus from the angular heap; 1 for using the evidence of sub-zero nights and water in the joints to explain freeze-thaw loosening; 1 for the interpretation that loosened fragments fall under gravity and accumulate at the foot.

before.canonical_answer: The exposed surface heats and expands differently from the interior. Cooling produces contraction and changing stresses. Repeated stress can grow surface-parallel fractures, allowing outer sheets to detach.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first differential heating/expansion step; 1 for cooling/contraction and stress change; 1 for fracture growth and sheet detachment as the result.

after.canonical_answer: The exposed surface heats and expands more than the interior by day. Cooling at night produces contraction and changing stresses. Repeated stress grows surface-parallel cracks until outer sheets detach, rounding the outcrop into an exfoliation dome with the fallen sheets collecting at its foot.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first step: differential heating/expansion of the outer layer; 1 for the next step: cooling/contraction and stress change; 1 for the result: fracture growth and sheet detachment, leaving a rounded dome with debris at its foot.

after.text: Less resistant rocks generally weather faster than more resistant ones under the same conditions; dark rocks absorb more heat and reach higher surface temperatures, and in coarse-grained rocks neighbouring crystals heat and expand by different amounts, which can loosen grains (granular disintegration).

before: Rock characteristics influence access and susceptibility. Mineral composition affects how readily a rock undergoes particular chemical reactions. Limestone contains calcium carbonate that can dissolve in weak carbonic acid; granite contains minerals with different susceptibilities, including feldspar that can alter by hydrolysis. It is misleading to call one rock universally weak and another universally strong without specifying the process. A material resistant to one kind of weathering may be vulnerable under another set of conditions. The relevant comparison is between the actual minerals, structure and environment.
after: Rock characteristics influence access and susceptibility. Mineral composition affects how readily a rock undergoes particular chemical reactions. Limestone contains calcium carbonate that can dissolve in weak carbonic acid; granite contains minerals with different susceptibilities, including feldspar that can alter by hydrolysis. Resistance matters too: under the same conditions, less resistant rocks generally break down faster than more resistant ones, although a rock that resists one process may be vulnerable to another. Colour and grain size affect heating. Dark rocks absorb more of the sun’s heat and reach higher surface temperatures. In coarse-grained rocks such as granite, neighbouring crystals of different minerals heat and expand by different amounts, which can loosen individual grains (granular disintegration). The relevant comparison is between the actual minerals, structure and environment.

before.prompt: Name one rock feature that gives water access to internal surfaces and can increase weathering.
before.canonical_answer: Open joints or connected fractures.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the name open joints/connected fractures.

after.prompt: Name one rock feature, other than joints, that affects how quickly a rock is weathered.
after.canonical_answer: Rock colour. Mineral composition, grain size, resistance (hardness) or permeability are also acceptable.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for naming one relevant rock feature: colour, mineral composition, grain size, resistance/hardness or permeability.

after.text: Equatorial rainforest climates are hot all year with an annual range of about 2°C because the midday sun is always high; strong heating makes moist air rise in the ITCZ low-pressure belt, where it cools and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds that give heavy convectional rain, often in the early afternoon, with high humidity and light surface winds.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that agroforestry is a better way than reforestation to reduce forest clearance in a farming area where families depend on crops and fuelwood?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Agroforestry keeps the land producing: trees grown among crops supply fuelwood, fodder and timber, so families need to cut less natural forest, while roots and leaf litter reduce soil erosion and nitrogen-fixing trees can raise fertility. Reforestation restores habitat and soil cover on cleared land, but it takes that land out of farming and gives little income until the trees are established, so families who need the land now may resist it. However, agroforestry needs effort, skill and secure land rights, and badly spaced trees compete with crops for water and light. Decision: in this setting agroforestry is the better first step, with reforestation best kept for steep or degraded land that is not farmed.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging relevant facts on both sides: fuelwood or fodder reducing clearance; soil protection or fertility; reforestation restoring habitat but removing farmland and giving slow returns; agroforestry needing skill, tenure and careful spacing.

Suitable aftercare and longer monitoring are needed for cover and wider functions. Some surviving growth is a benefit, but full restoration is not demonstrated.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that a reforestation project on a cleared, eroding hillside has been worthwhile? Native trees were replanted; after three years most survive and runoff from the slope has fallen, but local families have lost grazing on that hillside.
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Most planted trees have survived three years, so the project has moved beyond counting seedlings, and the fall in runoff shows the new cover is already protecting the soil and slowing water on the slope. Native species should also restore more habitat than a single exotic crop. However, three years is too short to show a mature mixed forest, and the families who lost grazing bear a real cost that could make them damage the young trees. Decision: worthwhile for soil and water so far, but long-term success needs continued monitoring and an alternative grazing or income arrangement for the affected families.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the survival evidence, the runoff and soil-protection benefit, the short time scale or habitat uncertainty, and the cost to families who lost grazing.

before: Leisure and tourist activities in Namibia include wildlife viewing, guided nature visits, walking, coastal recreation, heritage visits, cultural experiences and attending events. Their locations reflect the resources needed. Wildlife viewing depends on suitable wildlife opportunities and access; coastal recreation uses the coast; heritage visits depend on the relevant place and interpretation. The range of activities means that tourism is not confined to one attraction or one visitor motive.
after: Namibia's leisure and tourist activities use its landscapes, wildlife and culture. Visitors climb the red dunes and take photographs at Sossusvlei in the Namib-Naukluft National Park. Hikers walk the Fish River Canyon trail in the south during the cooler months, roughly May to mid-September. The coastal resort of Swakopmund offers quad biking, skydiving and beach holidays. Wildlife viewing takes place in national parks and in communal conservancies.

before: Etosha is a named example of nature-based tourism. The Ministry's park information describes game viewing and accommodation or camping services at park camps. These illustrate the connection between a wildlife attraction and the services enabling visits. They do not supply a current total of visitors, jobs or revenue, and no such total should be inferred from the existence of facilities.
after: Etosha National Park in northern Namibia was first proclaimed in 1907 and covers about 22,000 km². It is dominated by the Etosha Pan, a large salt pan that is usually dry, so wildlife depends on waterholes. Visitors take game drives, bird-watch and photograph animals at waterholes, including floodlit ones at the Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni rest camps, which provide chalets, camping, restaurants and guided drives.

before: Community-based tourism can include guiding, craft activities, campsites and joint-venture accommodation. The Ministry describes support for community enterprises and management skills. Such activities can provide income and opportunities to interpret local culture, while their benefits depend on participation, agreements and actual demand. A cultural activity should be described respectfully through the hosts' chosen presentation rather than as a spectacle imposed for outsiders.
after: Heritage visits include Twyfelfontein in the Kunene Region, Namibia's first World Heritage Site (2007), where guides show visitors ancient rock engravings. Community-based tourism offers guiding, craft sales, campsites and joint-venture lodges in conservancies, giving local people income from wildlife and culture when they control what is shared.

before: Activity choice affects environmental pressure and service demand. A walking route needs suitable path management; vehicle-based wildlife viewing needs access and behaviour rules; overnight stays require water and waste services. Compare the particular activity and setting rather than assuming all tourism has the same footprint. This links the activity examples to the benefits, costs and management questions developed below.
after: Residents also use local leisure facilities such as sports fields, parks and braai sites, and make holiday trips to the coast. Each activity needs particular services: hiking trails need path maintenance, game drives need roads and rules, and overnight stays need water and waste services.

after.prompt: “Poor transport is the main problem limiting the development of tourism in Namibia.” How far do you agree with this statement?
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. For the statement: attractions such as Etosha, Sossusvlei and Fish River Canyon are far apart and far from overseas markets; most roads are gravel or earth, so journeys are slow and costly; and air links were reduced when the national airline stopped flying in 2021, ending direct flights to Frankfurt. Against it: transport is only one constraint. Lodges also need capital for buildings, water and waste systems; marketing is needed to attract bookings; trained staff and good organisation are needed to deliver services; and seasonal demand leaves facilities underused. Decision: poor transport is a major problem, especially for remote sites, but it works together with capital, marketing and management problems, so it is not on its own the main problem.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using Namibian transport evidence (distance, gravel roads, air links) weighed against other constraints (capital, marketing, organisation, seasonality).

after.prompt: How far do you agree that a joint-venture lodge with a private investor is a good way for a community conservancy to overcome its lack of capital for tourism?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. The investor supplies the money and management skills to build and run a lodge that the community could not finance itself, and the conservancy can receive contractual payments, jobs and training without taking on loans. However, benefits depend on the agreement: payments may be small or late, senior jobs may go to outsiders, profits can leave the area, and the community gives up some control over how its land is used. Decision: largely a good way, provided the contract sets fair payments, local jobs and training and is monitored so that members actually receive the benefits.

before: A maximum thermometer records the highest temperature reached since its last reset, while a minimum thermometer records the lowest. A combined maximum–minimum or Six’s thermometer uses indices to preserve the extremes. The current liquid level is not necessarily the extreme indicated by an index. Read the labelled scale and the specified end of the index, because the orientation and arrangement of scales can differ. Reset only after recording, using the approved method for the particular instrument. A missing reset changes the period represented by the next observation, so it belongs in the record.
after: A maximum thermometer records the highest temperature reached since its last reset, and a minimum thermometer the lowest. A Six’s thermometer combines both in one U-shaped glass tube. Alcohol in the tube expands and contracts as the temperature changes and pushes a thread of mercury round the bend. The mercury pushes a small steel index along each arm, and each index stays at the furthest point it was pushed to. The maximum is read on the right-hand arm, whose scale reads upwards; the minimum on the left-hand arm, whose scale reads downwards. Read the end of each index nearest the mercury, with your eye level with it. The top of the mercury on either scale gives the current temperature. After recording, reset the thermometer by drawing each index back down onto the mercury with a magnet, or by pressing the release button on newer models. A missed reset changes the period that the next reading covers, so note it in the record.

The mercury shows the current temperature, 20°C, which is neither extreme. After recording, the indices are drawn back down onto the mercury with a magnet to reset the thermometer.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the feature that the right-hand index gives the maximum (28°C) and the left-hand index the minimum (12°C).
1 mark for using the mercury value (20°C) as evidence of the current temperature, distinct from the extremes.
1 mark for the reset: indices drawn back to the mercury with a magnet after recording.

before: A Stevenson screen is an instrument shelter designed to help measure representative air temperature and humidity while reducing direct effects of sunshine, precipitation and nearby heated surfaces. The familiar school model is a raised, white, louvred enclosure. Its slatted sides allow air circulation while shielding instruments. The white exterior reflects much incoming solar radiation, reducing heating of the shelter relative to a darker surface under similar conditions. A roof provides protection from direct radiation and precipitation; designs can include a double roof to reduce heat transfer. Modern shelters can use different materials, so the function should be understood rather than reduced to wood alone.

before: Altitude commonly influences temperature in the troposphere: higher sites are generally cooler than comparable lower sites. Rising air expands in lower surrounding pressure and cools, while the environmental temperature profile also reflects heating, mixing, radiation and atmospheric structure. A temperature inversion can reverse the usual decrease over a layer, so the relation is a broad tendency rather than an absolute rule for every height interval. A mountain summit and a sheltered valley floor may also have different local exposure and night-time conditions.
after: Altitude commonly influences temperature in the troposphere: higher sites are generally cooler than comparable lower sites. The main reason is that the lower atmosphere is heated mainly from below: sunlight warms the ground, and the ground then heats the air above it, so air farther above the land surface is cooler. Air at height is also thinner (less dense) and holds less heat. On average, temperature falls by about 6.5°C for each 1,000 m of height. A temperature inversion can reverse the usual decrease over a layer, so the relation is a broad tendency rather than an absolute rule for every height interval. A mountain summit and a sheltered valley floor may also have different local exposure and night-time conditions.

before: The Benguela system off southwestern Africa brings a cold marine influence along Namibia’s coast, with upwelling contributing to cool surface waters. Namibia’s coastal fog illustrates that visible moisture and limited rainfall can coexist. NASA accounts connect fog over the Namib with the cool coastal ocean and surrounding atmospheric conditions. This is a useful mechanism-based example, not a claim that the current alone explains the entire desert or that fog forms at the same intensity every day. Pressure-related subsidence and local weather also influence the vertical structure and persistence of the coastal layer.
after: The cold Benguela Current flows northward along Namibia’s coast, from higher latitudes towards the Equator, and upwelling brings cold water to the surface near the shore. Air over this cold water is cooled from below, so it becomes stable: it does not rise to form rain clouds, but its moisture often condenses into fog. This helps explain why the Namib coast is foggy yet very dry; average rainfall within 40 km of the coast is below 20 mm a year. The current does not explain the whole desert on its own, because sinking air in the subtropical high also keeps the air dry.

before: Large-scale convergence zones can move seasonally and help organise rainfall patterns in tropical and subtropical regions. Their influence at one location depends on how far the circulation shifts and on the regional geography. A summer-rainfall pattern in part of the southern African interior can be connected to seasonal moisture and ascent, while the coastal setting may retain stronger marine and stability controls. Do not assume that one monthly graph represents every place within Namibia. Local and regional records are needed to specify the pattern at the named site.
after: Air heated near the Equator rises, cools and loses its moisture as rain, then spreads towards the poles and sinks at about 30° north and south. The sinking air warms and dries, forming belts of subtropical high pressure, so many hot deserts, including the Namib, lie between about 15° and 30° from the Equator. The zone where air converges and rises near the Equator, the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), shifts south during the southern summer. It brings most of Namibia’s rain between about September and April, and the north-east receives on average more than 650 mm a year, far more than the coast. One monthly graph therefore does not represent every place in Namibia.

before.canonical_answer: Cold water cools near-surface marine air and can support fog under suitable moisture conditions. Subsidence can warm air aloft and inhibit deep cloud development. Together they can support cool foggy but low-rainfall conditions; latitude alone does not determine the result.

A teaching plan can use identical house symbols in three panels with the same orientation and scale. Panel A places eight houses apart across farm plots; B places eight along one east–west route; C groups eight around a crossroads. before: A settlement's function is the work or services it provides, such as farming support, trade, administration, industry, transport or tourism. Size and growth can reflect those roles alongside natural change, migration, land and services. A port or administrative centre can support jobs and attract residents, while an enterprise decline can reduce opportunities. A settlement may have several functions that change through time.
after: A settlement's site is the land it is built on, such as a dry point above flood level, a wet point near water or a defensive hill. Its situation is its position relative to surrounding places, routes and resources. Its function is the main work or services it provides. In Namibia, Windhoek is the capital and administrative centre, Walvis Bay is a port with the country's only natural deep-water harbour and a large fishing industry, Oranjemund is a diamond-mining town and Swakopmund is a beach resort.

before: Broad economic context influences resources and opportunities, but does not fix one function or growth rate for every settlement. Compare the actual employment, service and component evidence. A useful explanation distinguishes an observed increase, its possible causes and the service implications rather than assigning all change to migration or treating a city label as proof of prosperity.
after: Settlements grow when natural increase adds residents and when their functions create jobs and services that attract migrants. Rural–urban migration is driven by push factors in rural areas, such as drought, few jobs and poor services, and pull factors in towns, such as jobs, schools, hospitals and better services. Settlements decline when their function ends: Kolmanskop grew after diamonds were found in 1908 but was abandoned in 1956, after richer deposits near the Orange River drew people away.

before: Residential patterns can reflect transport, jobs, land prices, planning and historical inequality. Households with different resources may face different choices of space and location, while policy can improve or restrict access. Avoid treating every peripheral area as low income or every central area as affluent. Cities can contain contrasting neighbourhoods at similar distances from the centre.
after: Residential areas in MEDC cities are often described with the concentric zone model, which Ernest Burgess based on Chicago in 1925. Around the CBD lies a zone of transition with older factories and run-down housing, then inner suburbs of older, low-cost workers' housing, then outer suburbs of larger, newer middle-class homes, and finally a commuter zone. Wealthier people live farther from the centre, where land is cheaper, there is more space and less pollution, and they can afford to travel in by car or train.

before: A second comparison panel can show an older industrial corridor and inner housing around a central commercial area, with newer residential development and an edge shopping centre. It is a schematic MEDC comparison rather than a named city's measured history. Both panels can contain mixed uses, multiple shopping areas and inequalities. The broad LEDC/MEDC contexts do not establish a uniform residential or economic pattern.
after: Cities in LEDCs often show the reverse pattern. The wealthiest people live close to the CBD or along a main road leading out of it, in good-quality housing with full services and security. Middle-income housing lies farther out. The poorest people, many of them recent rural–urban migrants, live on the edge of the city in informal or squatter settlements, where land is unclaimed or cheap but services are few. Industry is often found along the main roads and railways leading out of the city.

before: The useful comparison focuses on common functions and the actual differences drawn. Both plans can show a CBD, housing, industry, transport and open space. They may differ in route alignment, edge expansion or the position of industry. Do not invent a high-rise income pattern or label all housing as formal or informal unless the key supplies it. A model's value is in the relationships it makes visible.
after: Windhoek shows parts of the LEDC pattern, shaped by its apartheid history. Black residents were forcibly moved from the Old Location to Katutura, about 8 km north of the centre, which was created in 1961. Today large informal settlements such as Havana have grown on the north-western edge, where many households share a few toilets and have limited water and legal electricity. Both models are generalisations: real cities contain exceptions, such as new wealthy estates on the edge of some LEDC cities.

before: The two schematic panels should use a common key so differences are meaningful. If one uses red for retail and the other for industry, a visual comparison can become misleading. Keep orientation and units clear, identify any scale difference and avoid using a colour as a claim about income. A comparison diagram teaches relationships; a map of a named city would require appropriate sourced geometry and current land-use evidence.
after: The main difference between the two models is the location of rich and poor housing. In MEDCs most low-income housing lies near the centre and most high-income housing in the suburbs; in LEDCs most high-income housing lies near the centre and low-income informal housing on the edge. In both, the CBD occupies the most accessible point and industry follows the main transport routes.

before: Windhoek provides a named upgrading case. City information describes a collaborative Informal Settlement Upgrading Project intended to support affordable housing on serviced land, while the National Housing Enterprise recorded a 2020 phase launch at Havana Proper. These sources establish the project and approach. They do not alone prove that every household is eligible, that all housing need has been met or that current delivery equals a historical target.
after: Windhoek provides a named upgrading case. City information describes a collaborative Informal Settlement Upgrading Project that supports affordable housing on serviced land, so that families can build on plots with water, sewerage and roads instead of in unplanned shacks. Upgrading of this kind keeps people near their jobs and neighbours, but plots, materials and loans must be affordable for the poorest households, and the city must keep pace with new arrivals.

before: A hypothetical upgrading project improves water and sanitation for fifty households but has no evidence about housing structures or tenure. It can claim those service improvements where delivery is verified, not completion of every housing objective. Another project may provide a legal document without a water connection. Evaluating components separately helps identify progress and the remaining practical need.
after: Informal settlements grow because migrants arrive faster than affordable serviced housing can be provided, and many cannot afford rent or plots in formal areas. Problems include shared or missing toilets and taps, illegal electricity connections, fire risk in closely packed shacks, flooding on low-lying land, disease and insecure tenure. Responses include site-and-service schemes, where plots with water, sewerage and roads are provided for people to build on, self-help housing with cheap materials or loans, and upgrading existing settlements in place.

before: Congestion measures also need a clear definition. A count at a junction records passage, while a queue length or journey-time record indicates delay under the stated conditions. A road may carry fewer vehicles when congestion is severe because flow is constrained. The relationship between count and congestion is therefore not simply more vehicles means proportionally more delay. Use the actual capacity and timing evidence.
after: Traffic congestion is common in the CBD because many roads converge there and many people travel in to work, shop and use services at the same times each day. Old CBD streets are often narrow, delivery vehicles stop to unload, cars park along the roadside or circle in search of parking, and where public transport is limited most people drive. Solutions include ring roads or bypasses to divert through-traffic, park-and-ride schemes, bus lanes, one-way streets, pedestrianised shopping streets and restricting large vehicles at busy times.

before: Velocity is speed of flow, commonly expressed in metres per second. Discharge is volume passing a cross-section per unit time, commonly cubic metres per second. The two are related through cross-sectional area but are not identical. A channel can become wider and deeper as discharge increases, so a change in volume does not determine velocity without considering channel geometry. after: Velocity is speed of flow, commonly expressed in metres per second. Discharge is volume passing a cross-section per unit time, commonly cubic metres per second. The two are related through cross-sectional area but are not identical. A channel can become wider and deeper as discharge increases, so a change in volume does not determine velocity without considering channel geometry. Likewise, a narrow constriction may have rapid flow even where the river’s overall gradient is gentle. Volume still matters for deposition. When the volume of water falls, the river has less energy and can no longer carry all its load, so it deposits some of it. Volume falls in the dry season and after a flood, when water evaporates in hot, dry areas, when it seeps into a sandy or permeable bed, and when people abstract it. Many Namibian rivers are ephemeral and lose water as they flow. During the floods studied on the Kuiseb River in the Namib, the water shrank downstream and all the transported material was deposited in the lower river; no water or sediment reached the Atlantic Ocean.

after.prompt: Explain how a fall in the volume of water can make an ephemeral river deposit its load as it flows across a sandy, permeable bed.

Flow paths, evaporation, infiltration and seasonal inundation can be important. Some inland systems terminate in pans or wetlands instead of maintaining one continuous channel to an ocean. after: An inland delta is a branching depositional system that spreads within an interior basin rather than building directly into the sea. Flow paths, evaporation, infiltration and seasonal inundation can be important. Some inland systems terminate in pans or wetlands instead of maintaining one continuous channel to an ocean. The broad term should not erase local distinctions between distributary networks, shallow seasonal channels and terminal depressions. The Okavango River rises in the highlands of Angola and crosses Namibia before spreading into many channels across the flat Kalahari basin. before.canonical_answer: Disagree with the claim. Dry appearance on one date does not remove the documented seasonal channel function. Building in the flow path creates exposure when water returns, and a road without openings could obstruct or redirect it. The alternative culvert crossing addresses connectivity more directly if its design is suitable and maintenance occurs. Seasonal records and actual flow paths should therefore guide siting; neither dry appearance nor a plan on paper proves safety.
