after.prompt: How far do you agree that the oshanas of the Cuvelai system bring more benefits than problems to the people who live among them? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. In the wet season the shallow oshanas fill with water that people use for livestock and household needs; they provide fish and support grazing and cultivation on the moist, low-lying ground, so many households depend on them. However, when large amounts of water flow in from Angola after heavy rain, oshanas can flood homes, schools, crops and roads, especially where people have built in channels that looked dry in earlier years. Standing water can also help spread disease where sanitation is poor, and roads without enough openings can make the flooding worse. The oshanas are a valuable resource, but whether the benefits outweigh the problems depends on the year and on where people build. With homes kept out of the flow paths and roads built with suitable culverts, the benefits can be greater than the problems.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging relevant evidence on both sides: benefits (seasonal water for livestock and households, fish, grazing, cultivation) and problems (flooding of homes, crops, schools and roads when inflow from Angola is high, building in dry channels, disease, obstruction by roads). Maximum 3 marks if only one side is judged.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision such as "partly agree", which may be implied; a bare agree or disagree earns no mark.

They do not establish that every plant in either town has identical costs or access, and changing capacity figures need dated sources. The example should explain why the infrastructure matters rather than rely on the place name alone.

before.prompt: Explain the link from coastal upwelling to a useful fish resource.
before.canonical_answer: Upwelling can bring nutrient-rich deeper water into the lit surface layer. Nutrients support phytoplankton where other needs are met. Consumers and fish use that production through food-web links, supporting resource availability over time.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for upwelling as the factor; 1 for the nutrient/sunlit-layer link; 1 for producer-to-consumer transfer; 1 for the conditional fish-resource effect.

after.prompt: Explain the link from coastal upwelling off Namibia to a useful fish resource.
after.canonical_answer: South-east trade winds push surface water away from Namibia’s coast, so cold, nutrient-rich water rises from depth into the sunlit surface layer. The nutrients support rapid phytoplankton growth. Zooplankton and fish feed on this production through the food chain, so large fish stocks can be supported over time.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: south-east trade winds moving surface water offshore, causing upwelling; 1 for the link: nutrient-rich water reaching the sunlit layer; 1 for the link because producers are eaten by zooplankton and fish; 1 for the effect: large fish stocks supported over time.

before.prompt: Describe what a coastline-length record can establish if it gives kilometres but no habitat, productivity or stock data.
before.canonical_answer: It establishes coastal extent, not a uniform fish density. Resource availability also needs habitat/productivity evidence. A sustainable-catch ranking cannot be calculated from length alone.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the extent feature; 1 for the missing-resource evidence; 1 for the limit on catch inference.

after.prompt: Namibia’s coastline is about 1,500 km long, from the Kunene River to the Orange River. Describe how this length affects the availability of fish, and one limit of using length alone.
after.canonical_answer: A long coastline gives a large sea area to fish and, with a 200-nautical-mile EEZ along it, very large fishing grounds over the Benguela upwelling zone. It also provides sites for fishing ports such as Walvis Bay and Lüderitz. Length alone does not show how many fish there are: productivity, habitat and stock size also matter.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the feature: a large fishing area or EEZ over the upwelling zone; 1 for the evidence of port or landing sites along the coast; 1 for the limit that length is not a measure of productivity or stock.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that a quota alone proves sustainable use? The limit fits a supplied assessment, but actual recorded catch exceeds it and pollution observations remain unresolved. Judge extraction and wider resource condition.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with proof. A suitable limit is relevant, but excess actual catch shows a compliance problem. Pollution is another unresolved pathway. Sustainable use needs effective removal control and relevant environmental assessment, not the quota’s presence alone.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the assessment, actual-catch evidence, compliance mechanism and unresolved environmental pressure.
1 C mark for a supported decision against the stated resource criterion.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that Namibia’s fisheries management has made its fish resources sustainable?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to some extent. Since 1990 the 200-nautical-mile EEZ has ended uncontrolled foreign fishing, and fishing rights, licences and yearly TACs set from scientific advice limit the catch. Observers on every commercial vessel, patrols and inspection of landings make the limits enforceable, while closed seasons and minimum mesh sizes protect breeding and young fish. However, rules cannot control the ocean: the 1993–1995 Benguela Niño, on top of earlier overfishing, reduced pilchard so far that its quota was set at zero for 2002. Quotas also protect stocks only if they are set at the right level and obeyed. Decision: management is strong and has protected most stocks, but environmental shocks mean sustainability is not guaranteed.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging relevant evidence on both sides: EEZ control; rights, licences and TACs; observers and patrols; closed seasons or mesh rules; the pilchard decline from the Benguela Niño and earlier overfishing; quotas needing correct levels and compliance.
1 C mark for a supported decision, which may be implied.

before.prompt: Name the pressure involving excessive removal relative to sustainable stock recovery.
before.canonical_answer: Overfishing.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the name overfishing.

after.prompt: Name the group whose largely unmanaged fishing overexploited Namibia’s fishing grounds before independence in 1990.
after.canonical_answer: Foreign distant-water fishing fleets.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the name: foreign (distant-water) fishing fleets.

before.prompt: Explain why fishing employment alone is not sufficient evidence of sustainable development.
before.canonical_answer: Jobs can support incomes, but continued benefit depends on the resource and viable operations. Excess extraction or unmanaged pollution can undermine future supply and functions. Sustainable-development judgement needs those linked conditions, not one employment count alone.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for employment as a benefit factor; 1 for the resource-continuity link; 1 for a pressure affecting recovery; 1 for its longer-term development effect.

after.prompt: Explain how Namibia’s policy of promoting onshore fish processing supports sustainable development.
after.canonical_answer: Much of the hake catch must be landed fresh for processing on shore, so filleting and packing take place in Walvis Bay and Lüderitz rather than at sea. This creates jobs and skills for Namibians and adds value before export, so more income from each tonne stays in the country. Because the catch is already limited by TACs, extra benefit comes from processing rather than from catching more fish, supporting people now while protecting stocks for the future.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: required onshore processing of part of the catch; 1 for the link: local jobs, skills and value added; 1 for the link because the catch is capped by TACs; 1 for the effect: more benefit without increasing catch, supporting long-term use.

before.prompt: Explain the error in classifying a filleting/freezing plant as primary just because it uses fish. Compare it with catching fish and transporting packages.
before.canonical_answer: The confusion classifies by raw material instead of activity. Catching is primary, processing is secondary and transport tertiary. The test identifies extraction, transformation or service in the described operation.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the material/activity confusion; 1 for the correct three-way distinction applied as a test.

after.prompt: A learner writes: “Secondary industry means second-hand trading, such as selling used boat engines.” Explain the error, then classify catching hake, canning pilchards and selling used engines.
after.canonical_answer: Secondary does not mean second-hand: it is the processing or manufacturing of raw materials into products. Catching hake is primary because it extracts a natural resource, canning pilchards is secondary because it processes fish, and selling used engines is tertiary because it is a trade service, whatever the age of the goods.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the error: secondary means processing or manufacturing, not second-hand goods.
1 mark for the correct classification used as a test: catching hake primary, canning pilchards secondary, selling used engines tertiary.

before.prompt: Describe the rural comparison: A clusters near a shared water point and school; B has homes on separate farm plots with road links. Rainfall is stated equal.
before.canonical_answer: A has shared-node concentration and B dispersed plot-related locations. The evidence supplies water/service and land-organisation differences despite equal rainfall. It does not establish different household wealth.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the paired pattern; 1 for the matched-rain/different-arrangement evidence; 1 for the bounded explanation.

after.prompt: Settlement A: homes clustered around a shared water point and school. Settlement B: homes on separate farm plots, each joined to a road. Both areas receive the same rainfall. Describe the difference in pattern and the evidence that explains it.
after.canonical_answer: A is nucleated and B is dispersed. Because rainfall is equal, it cannot explain the difference; the evidence points to the shared water point and school drawing homes together at A, and to separate farm plots with road access allowing homes to spread out at B.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the pattern: A nucleated, B dispersed.
1 mark for evidence that shared services explain A's clustering and separate plots explain B's spacing.
1 mark for using the equal-rainfall data to rule out rainfall as the cause.

before.prompt: Explain how a new usable employment function can support settlement growth where housing and access permit.
before.canonical_answer: The function creates livelihood opportunities and demand for related services. People may move towards those opportunities, adding to local population and service needs. Actual growth also depends on other components and available capacity.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for employment as a factor; 1 for the livelihood/service link; 1 for possible residential movement; 1 for the conditional growth effect.

after.prompt: Explain how a mining function can cause a settlement to grow and later decline.
after.canonical_answer: The discovery of a mineral such as diamonds is the factor that creates mining jobs, which attract migrants, and their spending supports shops and services, so the settlement grows. When the deposit is worked out or richer deposits are found elsewhere, mining stops, jobs are lost and people leave, so the settlement declines, as Kolmanskop did after 1928 until it was abandoned in 1956.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: a mineral discovery creating mining jobs.
1 mark for the link: jobs attract migrants because of work and income, supporting services.
1 mark for the result: the end of mining causes job losses.
1 mark for the effect of out-migration and decline, with an example such as Kolmanskop.

before.prompt: Name the urban zone with a concentration of commercial and business functions.

marking_guidance: 1 mark for the zone name CBD.

after.prompt: Name the part of a typical LEDC city where most informal (squatter) settlements are found.
after.canonical_answer: The urban fringe (the edge or outskirts of the city).
marking_guidance: 1 mark for naming the feature: urban fringe/edge/outskirts.

before.prompt: Name the CBD access problem indicated by queues or delays when movement exceeds usable space/capacity.
before.canonical_answer: Congestion.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the problem name congestion.

after.prompt: Name one cause of traffic congestion in a CBD.
after.canonical_answer: Many roads converge on the CBD. Also accept: many people travelling in at the same time, narrow old streets, delivery vehicles unloading, roadside parking or limited public transport.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for naming a relevant cause (point).

before.prompt: Name one transport measure that can reduce a specific car-access pressure where it is reliable, affordable and useful for relevant journeys.
before.canonical_answer: Suitable public transport or a relevant managed-demand/access measure.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for a relevant measure name.

after.prompt: Name a road built to divert through-traffic away from a town centre.
after.canonical_answer: A ring road or bypass.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for naming the feature: ring road or bypass.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that the cheapest housing charge is the most affordable complete option? Monthly housing/transport/services costs are A N$900/600/300 and B N$1,000/200/200; other costs and quality are unspecified.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree from those costs. A totals N$1,800 and B N$1,400, so A’s lower housing charge is outweighed by transport and service costs. B is lower for the stated bundle, but complete suitability and affordability require the remaining costs, income and conditions.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the cost evidence, both totals and the bundle-versus-housing distinction.
1 C mark for a supported bounded affordability decision.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that building a ring road is the best way to reduce traffic congestion in a CBD?
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. A ring road diverts through-traffic that does not need to enter the centre, so fewer vehicles use the narrow CBD streets and lorries can avoid the centre. However, it does nothing for the many people who travel into the CBD to work and shop, it is expensive and takes land, and new roads can attract more traffic. Measures aimed at CBD-bound traffic, such as better public transport, park-and-ride, bus lanes, pedestrianised streets and restrictions on large vehicles, are also needed. A ring road helps most where through-traffic is a large share of the congestion, but it is best combined with these measures.
marking_guidance: Up to 2 C marks for evidence of how a ring road reduces congestion.
Up to 2 C marks for limitations with reasons, or alternative measures for CBD-bound traffic.
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

before.prompt: Explain the error in concluding that a tall residential building proves high income or quality of life. What evidence discriminates form from living conditions?
before.canonical_answer: The confusion treats building height as household welfare. Occupancy, affordability, services and appropriate household evidence are needed; height alone describes form. Compare those conditions to test the social claim.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the form/welfare confusion; 1 for the correct distinction and relevant living-condition test.

after.prompt: Area X has twelve-storey blocks of flats where 40% of households lack piped water. Area Y has single-storey houses where 98% of households have piped water. Explain the error in concluding that Area X has the higher quality of life because its buildings are taller. What evidence discriminates between the areas?
after.canonical_answer: The error is the confusion of building height with living conditions: height describes the form of buildings, not the wellbeing of the people living in them. The correct distinction uses service and household indicators, and here the piped-water data point the other way, showing better conditions in Area Y. The test is to compare indicators such as access to water, sanitation, overcrowding and income rather than the number of storeys.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the confusion/error of using height as a measure of quality of life.
1 mark for the correct distinction using the piped-water data, with a test based on living-condition indicators.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that Windhoek’s Informal Settlement Upgrading Project title alone proves all housing needs are met? City information describes collaborative affordable-housing work on serviced land, and NHE recorded a 2020 phase launch at Havana Proper. This resource supplies no complete current need, affordability or household-outcome account. Judge the evidence. [5]
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with the complete-success claim. The sources establish a project and approach, not a reconciled current housing outcome for every household. Suitable structures, usable services, affordability, location and continuing need require appropriate records. Upgrading can contribute while a wider gap remains. A historical launch or project name is not proof of completed citywide delivery.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the case evidence, launch/outcome distinction and missing affordability/service/need records.
1 C mark for a supported decision recognising potential contribution without claiming all needs met.

after.prompt: Windhoek's Informal Settlement Upgrading Project supports affordable housing on serviced land. How far do you agree that upgrading informal settlements where they are is better than moving residents to new housing schemes elsewhere? [5]
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Upgrading in place keeps people close to their jobs, schools, relatives and neighbours, so livelihoods and support networks are not broken, and adding water, toilets, roads and electricity to an existing area is usually cheaper than building whole new towns. Collaborative projects such as Windhoek's let residents help plan the work. However, some settlements are on land that floods or is too densely packed to service safely, so some families may need to move, and upgraded plots and loans must still be affordable for the poorest. Upgrading is generally the better approach, with relocation used only where a site is unsafe.
marking_guidance: Up to 3 C marks for evidence supporting upgrading in place (jobs, networks, cost, participation).
Up to 1 C mark for a reason relocation may be needed (flood risk, density) or for affordability limits.
1 C mark for a reasoned overall judgement.

after: Seif (linear) dunes are found in the dune belt near Swakopmund, and linear dunes dominate inland across much of the Namib Sand Sea. Variety choice alone does not remove those limits; local performance evidence and a feasible input plan are needed. The record does not quantify the eventual harvest.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that high-yielding varieties (HYVs) are the best way to increase maize output on large commercial farms in the Maize Triangle?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent where water and nutrients are reliable. HYVs can produce more grain per hectare than older varieties, so output rises without more land; the Maize Triangle has both rain-fed and irrigated maize, and irrigated fields can meet their needs. However, HYVs reach their potential only with enough water, fertiliser and pest control, which add costs; in a dry season rain-fed fields may not benefit; and purchased seed raises costs. Decision: very effective on irrigated, well-managed fields, but less reliable on rain-fed land, so they work best combined with irrigation and suitable fertiliser.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: higher yield potential weighed against dependence on water, fertiliser and pest control, rain-fed risk and costs.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that this irrigation change reduces total applied water? Application falls from 1,000 to 700 m³ per hectare while area rises from two to four hectares in the same interval.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree for total water. The totals are 2,000 m³ before and 2,800 m³ after: an 800 m³ increase. The per-hectare measure improves, but expansion outweighs it. Sustainable abstraction also needs evidence about the source and other users.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the numerical evidence in both totals, the 800 m³ increase and efficiency-versus-total-use distinction.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that switching from surface (flood) irrigation to drip irrigation improved this farm's water management? Application fell from 1,000 to 700 m³ per hectare, while the irrigated area grew from two to four hectares in the same period. The water comes from a borehole whose level is falling.
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Drip irrigation delivers water close to the roots with less evaporation, and use per hectare fell by 300 m³ (30%), so efficiency improved. However, total use rose from 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 m³ to 700 × 4 = 2,800 m³, an increase of 800 m³, because the area doubled, and the falling borehole level suggests abstraction is greater than recharge. Decision: water efficiency improved, but overall water management did not, unless the irrigated area is limited to what the source can sustain.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: the 30% per-hectare saving and drip mechanism weighed against the 800 m³ rise in total use and the falling borehole.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that repeated use of one pesticide proves lasting pest control? Damage fell initially, then the target population survived the same treatment more often; no monitoring or alternative measures are planned.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with lasting control being established. The initial benefit is evidence, but later survival raises a resistance concern and weakens the continuing-control claim. Monitoring and suitable integrated measures are needed. The record suggests a problem rather than proving a precise resistance mechanism by itself.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the early benefit, later evidence, resistance concern and need for monitored suitable control.
1 C mark for a supported decision about lasting rather than initial success.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that spraying insecticides is the best way for a large commercial vegetable farm to reduce crop losses to insects?
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Insecticides act quickly against a damaging outbreak and protect the yield and quality of produce for sale. However, repeated use of the same product can make pests resistant; sprays can kill pollinators and natural predators and can wash into water; and they cost money and need safe handling. Integrated pest management, which monitors pests, uses crop rotation and natural predators and sprays only when damage justifies it, can protect yields more sustainably. Decision: insecticides are useful within a managed approach, but used alone they are not the best long-term method.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: fast protection of yield weighed against resistance, non-target and pollution effects, cost, and integrated pest management as an alternative.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before.prompt: Explain a pathway from repeated heavy grazing with inadequate recovery to reduced future agricultural capacity.
before.canonical_answer: Grazing removes cover faster than regrowth replaces it. Exposed or compacted ground can have more runoff and soil loss under suitable storm conditions. Reduced soil and forage recovery can then lower future grazing resources.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for grazing pressure as a factor; 1 for the cover/recovery link; 1 for the soil/runoff mechanism; 1 for the later capacity effect.

after.prompt: Explain how drilling new boreholes in a communal grazing area of northern Namibia can lead to land degradation around the water points.
after.canonical_answer: More water allows more livestock to be kept, and the animals gather near the boreholes. Grazing and trampling remove grass faster than it can regrow and compact the soil. The bare ground is then eroded by wind and runoff. Less grass and soil reduce future grazing and contribute to desertification.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: boreholes allowing more livestock that concentrate at water points.
1 mark for the link: grazing and trampling remove grass faster than it regrows.
1 mark for the link to bare, compacted soil eroded by wind or water.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that a drought-tolerant bred variety eliminates drought risk? It performs better under moderate stress but still fails in an independently recorded severe water shortage.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with elimination. The moderate-stress comparison supports a conditional benefit, while failure under severe shortage shows a remaining limit. Suitability and water management remain relevant. Tolerance is not immunity or freedom from other input needs.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that breeding drought-tolerant mahangu varieties is a sustainable strategy for farmers in northern Namibia?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Rainfall in northern Namibia is unreliable, and varieties that tolerate dry spells or mature within the short rainy season keep yields more stable without extra water or chemicals, so the strategy suits the resources farmers have. However, tolerance is not immunity: a severe drought can still cause crop failure; improved seed must reach farmers at an affordable price; and soil fertility and good practice are still needed. Decision: a sustainable strategy, most effective when combined with soil and water conservation.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: more stable yields under dry spells and low input needs weighed against severe drought, seed access and other needs.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before.canonical_answer: Disagree for this stated mass criterion: the mixture totals 1,100 kg, 100 kg below 1,200 kg. It diversifies products, but diversification does not prove a greater combined mass. Nutritional value, income or risk could yield different judgements and need their own evidence.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that mixed cropping of maize with beans is better than growing maize alone? On the same area in the same season, the mixture gave 800 kg of maize plus 300 kg of beans, and maize alone gave 1,200 kg.
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. On total edible mass alone, maize grown alone did better: the mixture gave 800 + 300 = 1,100 kg, 100 kg less than 1,200 kg. However, the mixture gives two foods for a more varied diet, spreads the risk if one crop fails, keeps more ground covered, and the beans, as a legume, can add nitrogen that helps later crops. Decision: better for food security and soil sustainability, but not if the only aim is the largest grain harvest this season.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: the 1,100 kg against 1,200 kg comparison weighed against diet, risk-spreading, cover and nitrogen benefits.

before.canonical_answer: Disagree as written: the plan has a three-tonne material gap and a competing-use constraint. after.prompt: How far do you agree that using kraal manure as organic fertiliser is a sustainable way to improve mahangu yields in northern Namibia?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Many northern households keep cattle, so manure costs little; it returns nutrients and organic matter, improving the structure and water-holding capacity of sandy soils. However, its nutrient content varies and is released slowly; carrying bulky manure from the kraal to the fields takes labour; there may not be enough for every field; and badly stored manure can pollute water. Decision: a sustainable, low-cost strategy where enough manure is available, best combined with other nutrient sources and careful storage.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence: low cost, nutrients and soil-structure benefits weighed against variable nutrients, labour, limited supply and pollution risk.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before: Documentary data can provide a control or historical comparison, but only where the methods fit. A beach survey made after a storm may not be comparable with a calm-season record if the question assumes matched conditions. A visitor series can change because the entrance counter or definition changed. Read the source notes and retain those limitations rather than use the longer record simply because it contains more numbers.
after: Standard field equipment includes a tape measure for distances and widths; ranging poles, tall striped poles held upright to mark points; a clinometer to measure slope angles; a ruler or callipers to measure pebble length; a stopwatch to time counts; a tally sheet or hand counter to record counts; a quadrat, a square frame for sampling vegetation or beach material; and a float to measure the speed of water or the direction of drift. A compass gives direction and a camera keeps a visual record.

before: A field team should agree roles before a timed observation. One person can watch a defined line while another records, with a later check against categories and duration. Swapping roles can reveal inconsistent rules, but should not alter the counting definition. Record interruptions, obstructed views and unusual events rather than silently treating the interval as fully observed. A missed part of a count cannot be replaced with an invented average unless the estimate and its assumptions are explicitly labelled.
after: To measure beach gradient, place one ranging pole at the first point and a second pole a measured distance down the beach, using the tape. Sight the clinometer from a mark on the upper pole to the same height on the lower pole, then read and record the angle; repeat down to the water's edge to build a beach profile. To measure the width of a stream, place a ranging pole on each bank and measure between them with a tape held straight and at right angles to the channel.

after.prompt: Describe how to measure the gradient of a beach between two points using ranging poles, a tape measure and a clinometer.

before.prompt: Explain why naming a tape measure alone is not a reproducible path-width method.

after.prompt: Explain why a stopwatch and a tally sheet are used together in a pedestrian count.
after.canonical_answer: The stopwatch makes each count last exactly the same time at every site, because totals can only be compared if the periods match. The tally sheet records each person the moment they pass, so none are forgotten and the total can be checked afterwards.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the reason for the stopwatch: equal, timed periods so counts are comparable.
1 mark for the reason for the tally: recording each passage as it happens because memory would miss some.

after.prompt: Explain why twenty resident and twenty visitor respondents do not prove the wider population is half residents and half visitors.

before: A representative fraction gives the ratio, while a scale bar shows labelled ground distances graphically. Both must match the displayed map. If a page is resized, a printed fraction alone no longer describes a ruler measurement at the original size; a scale bar resized with the image retains a usable relationship. On-screen zoom can change centimetres measured on the screen, so use a valid supplied bar or the intended print dimensions for distance tasks.
after: Scale can be shown in three ways. A representative fraction (RF), such as 1:50 000, is a ratio with no units. A linear scale, or scale bar, is a line divided into labelled ground distances. A statement scale, or word scale, gives the relationship in words, such as "1 cm represents 0.5 km". To convert 1:50 000, note that 1 cm represents 50 000 cm; divide by 100 to get 500 m, then by 1 000 to get 0.5 km. If a map is resized on a screen, only the scale bar stays correct, because it changes size with the map.

A ridge is a long narrow stretch of high ground; a saddle is a lower dip between two hills; a gorge is a deep valley with very close contours on both sides; and an inselberg is an isolated steep-sided hill rising from a plain.

before.prompt: Describe the hydroelectric generation sequence from directed water to electrical supply.
before.canonical_answer: Water moves through a usable head and turns a turbine; the connected generator converts rotation into electricity; electrical equipment and connections deliver supply while water continues downstream.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first water/turbine step; 1 for generator conversion; 1 for the separated water and electrical-output result.

after.prompt: Describe the hydroelectric generation sequence from the water intake to the electricity supply.
after.canonical_answer: Water enters the intake and falls through the penstock, gaining speed; the moving water turns the turbine, whose shaft spins the generator to produce electricity; a transformer and power lines carry the electricity to users while the water leaves through the tailrace.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for intake/penstock and the falling water turning the turbine; 1 for the turbine driving the generator to produce electricity; 1 for transmission by power lines with the water leaving through the tailrace.

before.canonical_answer: (a) Photovoltaic/PV. (b) Directed water through head turns a turbine; the connected generator converts rotation to electricity; suitable electrical connections deliver it while water exits downstream. (c) Coal, oil or natural gas. (d) Solar rises as hydro falls; combined output stays eight units per month.

after.canonical_answer: (a) Photovoltaic/PV. (b) Water falls through the penstock and turns the turbine; the turbine spins the generator, which produces electricity; power lines carry the electricity away while the water leaves through the tailrace. (c) Coal, oil or natural gas. (d) Solar rises as hydro falls; combined output stays eight units per month.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that Ruacana’s renewable source proves constant output in every month? NamPower identifies it as run-of-the-river hydropower, and usable flow varies. Judge dependable generation.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with constant output being established. Renewable river supply does not mean constant usable flow. Run-of-river generation remains constrained by that flow and operating conditions; a maximum rating or the source label cannot replace actual generation evidence.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the case’s design evidence, flow dependence and rating/output distinction.
1 C mark for a supported dependable-generation decision.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that hydroelectric power from Ruacana on the Kunene River is the best way for Namibia to produce its electricity?
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Ruacana uses a renewable river flow, has no fuel costs and releases no smoke or carbon dioxide while generating, and the Kunene supplies up to 45 per cent of Namibia's electricity. However, Ruacana is a run-of-river station with little storage, so its output falls when the Kunene is low in the dry season, and the river's flow depends on rain in Angola. One station also cannot meet all of Namibia's demand. Ruacana is a valuable part of the supply, but Namibia also needs other sources such as solar power and imports.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement weighing Ruacana's advantages (renewable flow, no fuel cost or emissions during generation, large share of supply) against its limits (run-of-river, low dry-season flow, flow from Angola, cannot meet all demand).
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. partly agree because Ruacana is important but must be combined with other sources.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that a coal generator’s presence alone establishes dependable supply? Its equipment works but no fuel is available and no delivery is arranged.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree. Conversion capacity exists, but the required fuel input is absent. A usable continuing fuel chain is needed alongside equipment and connections. Dependability is not established by ownership or maximum capacity alone.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the functioning-equipment evidence, absent input and supply-chain conditions.
1 C mark for a supported decision against established supply.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that the disadvantages of generating electricity from coal outweigh its advantages?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Coal stations give a steady, controllable output, and coal can be stockpiled and is plentiful in some countries. However, burning coal releases carbon dioxide, which adds to the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming, and sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which cause acid rain that damages forests, lakes and fish. Mining damages land, ash must be disposed of, and coal is finite. The advantages are mainly short-term reliability, while the disadvantages are long-lasting and affect the whole planet.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement weighing coal's advantages (reliable controllable output, can be stockpiled, plentiful in some countries) against its disadvantages (CO2 and global warming, SO2/NOx and acid rain, mining damage, ash, finite).
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. agree to a large extent because the environmental costs outweigh reliability.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that low direct operating carbon emissions make nuclear power renewable and free of waste responsibilities? It uses finite uranium and produces radioactive materials requiring management.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree. Low direct carbon emissions describe one operating characteristic, not fuel replenishment. Finite uranium remains non-renewable, while radioactive-material and decommissioning responsibilities remain. The emissions benefit is real without establishing those separate claims.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the emissions/replenishment distinction and supplied waste evidence.
1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting the combined claim.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that nuclear power is too dangerous to be used for generating electricity?
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Accidents can be very serious: in March 2011 an earthquake and tsunami cut the cooling at Japan's Fukushima Daiichi station, three reactor cores melted and about 110,000 people were evacuated because of radiation. Radioactive waste must also be stored safely for a very long time. However, serious accidents are rare, modern stations have strong safety systems, and nuclear power gives a large, steady output with very little carbon dioxide during operation. The danger is real, but with strict safety controls nuclear power can still be used where the risk is managed.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement weighing dangers (accident risk illustrated by Fukushima 2011, radioactive waste) against benefits (rare accidents, safety systems, large steady low-carbon output).
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. partly agree.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that a solar store charged with ten energy units can supply a ten-unit evening load? Under the stated losses only eight units can be delivered, and no other supply is available.
before.canonical_answer: Disagree: deliverable energy is eight units, leaving a two-unit gap. Storage shifts energy with losses; it does not create the missing amount. Adequacy also depends on timing and discharge power, which would need to match the load.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using input/delivered evidence, the two-unit deficit and relevant storage conditions.
1 C mark for a supported decision against full-load coverage.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that solar power is the most suitable energy source for rural households far from Namibia's national grid?
after.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Namibia is very sunny, solar home systems need no power lines to be built and no fuel to be bought, and they produce no smoke; the Off-Grid Energisation Master Plan (2007) aimed to supply such households mainly with solar energy. However, panels and batteries are expensive to buy, output stops at night unless batteries are used, and small systems power lights, radios and phones but not cooking. Solar is the best source for lighting and small appliances, but many households will still need wood or gas for cooking.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement weighing solar's advantages (abundant sunshine, no grid or fuel needed, no smoke, supported by off-grid policy) against its limits (high upfront cost, no output at night without batteries, cannot power cooking).
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. agree to a large extent with cooking as the main limitation.

before.prompt: Explain how dependable usable energy can support a small food enterprise where refrigeration is needed.
before.canonical_answer: Suitable power and energy allow refrigeration to operate at required times. This can reduce temperature-related spoilage under appropriate handling, retaining more saleable food. The benefit depends on affordability, functioning equipment and the service actually supplied.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for dependable supply as a factor; 1 for the refrigeration link; 1 for reduced spoilage under suitable conditions; 1 for the usable-output effect.

after.prompt: Explain why Namibia's energy policy aims to increase the amount of electricity generated from local renewable sources.
after.canonical_answer: Namibia generates less than half of the electricity it uses and imports the rest from neighbouring countries. Imports cost money that leaves the country and may be cut if suppliers are short of power. Building local solar and other renewable stations uses Namibia's own resources, such as strong sunshine, which improves security of supply, a goal of the energy policy, and can bring electricity and jobs to rural areas.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for dependence on imported electricity as a factor; 1 for the cost or supply-risk link; 1 for local renewable resources (e.g. sunshine) improving security of supply; 1 for a wider development effect such as rural access or jobs.

before.prompt: Explain how a global oil-price increase can affect a country relying on imported petroleum products.
before.canonical_answer: Higher world supply costs can raise import costs, with the local effect also depending on exchange rates and domestic arrangements. Delivered fuel can then become more costly for transport or machinery, affecting users and supply chains. An exact retail change needs current local evidence.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for world price as a factor; 1 for the import-cost link; 1 for delivered-use costs; 1 for the conditional wider economic effect.

after.prompt: Explain how a rise in world oil prices affects Namibia.
after.canonical_answer: Namibia has no oil refinery, so it imports all its petrol and diesel, mainly through Walvis Bay. When world oil prices rise, the fuel import bill rises, so pump prices go up. Higher transport and diesel costs then raise the cost of moving goods, mining, farming and running generators, which pushes up prices for consumers.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for Namibia importing all refined fuel (no refinery); 1 for the higher import bill; 1 for higher pump/fuel prices; 1 for a wider effect on transport, production or consumer prices.

before.prompt: Describe what a regional electricity map establishes when it shows a transmission connection but no available-capacity or contract figures.
before.canonical_answer: It shows a route for potential exchange. It does not show the quantity available at each time or unlimited import capability. Supply, agreements and network conditions are needed to assess dependable delivery.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the connection pattern; 1 for the map’s present/missing evidence; 1 for the bounded exchange interpretation.

after.prompt: A map shows the Caprivi Link, a 950 km power line opened in 2010, running from Gerus in central Namibia to Katima Mulilo in the north-east, near the borders with Zambia and Zimbabwe. Describe what it shows about Namibia's electricity links with other SADC countries.
after.canonical_answer: The line joins Namibia's central grid to the far north-east, close to Zambia and Zimbabwe. It connects Namibia to the northern part of the Southern African Power Pool, so electricity can be imported from countries other than South Africa. This makes Namibia less dependent on one supplier.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the route/connection pattern (central Namibia to the north-east border area); 1 for linking to Zambia/Zimbabwe and the regional power pool; 1 for the interpretation of more supply options or less dependence on South Africa.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that Ruacana’s existence proves Namibia needs no other electricity source or regional exchange? NamPower identifies Ruacana as run-of-the-river hydropower. River flow and electricity demand vary, and no complete generation/demand time series or storage provision is supplied here. Judge adequacy and diversity of supply. [5]
before.canonical_answer: Disagree that the conclusion is established. Ruacana provides a renewable contribution, but run-of-river output depends on usable flow and cannot be credited with unprovided seasonal storage. Demand varies too, and the missing matched time series prevents an adequacy conclusion. Other domestic sources, suitable storage or regional exchange can contribute under their own conditions. Their necessity or precise quantity must be assessed from actual supply and demand rather than the existence of one station.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the case design, flow dependence, demand/time evidence gap and conditional system alternatives.
1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting the unsupported self-sufficiency inference.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that Namibia should continue to rely on imported electricity from other SADC countries rather than build more of its own power stations? Use Ruacana and Namibia's regional links in your answer. [5]
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Namibia generates less than half of the electricity it uses, and Ruacana, its main hydroelectric station, produces less when the Kunene is low in the dry season, so imports through the Southern African Power Pool, including the Caprivi Link to Zambia and Zimbabwe, fill the gap and can be cheaper than new stations. However, imports cost money that leaves the country and depend on spare power in partner countries. The energy policy aims for security of supply by using local resources, and Namibia has strong sunshine for solar power. Namibia should keep its regional links but also build more local renewable generation.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using Ruacana's seasonal limit, the import share and regional links (SAPP, Caprivi Link), and the costs/risks of imports against local options such as solar and the security-of-supply goal.
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. partly agree: keep imports while expanding local generation.

before.prompt: Describe the source contrast: A is an aquifer reached by a borehole; B is a reservoir, and neither record supplies quality tests or operating yields.
before.canonical_answer: A stores groundwater in suitable material and B stores surface water. The borehole is an access point, while the reservoir is a surface store. Their existence alone does not establish safe quality or dependable usable output.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the source-category relationship; 1 for access/store evidence; 1 for the quality/yield limit.

after.prompt: A map of Namibia's water sources shows perennial rivers only along the northern, north-eastern and southern borders, many ephemeral river beds across the interior, and productive aquifers in the Karstveld, at Stampriet and in Ohangwena. Describe the pattern of water sources shown.
after.canonical_answer: Permanent surface water is found only at the edges of the country, along the border rivers. The interior has only ephemeral rivers, which flow briefly after rain, so most places away from the borders depend on groundwater from aquifers such as those in the Karstveld, at Stampriet and in Ohangwena.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the pattern of perennial rivers only on the borders; 1 for map evidence that interior rivers are ephemeral; 1 for the interpretation that the interior depends mainly on groundwater, with a named aquifer area.

before.prompt: Explain how a water source can retain water while a settlement temporarily loses access.
before.canonical_answer: A pump, treatment or delivery interruption can break the source-to-user chain. Water remains in the source but cannot reach users in the required form or time. The response must address the interrupted stage rather than assume physical exhaustion.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for infrastructure interruption as a factor; 1 for the chain link; 1 for the usable-access effect; 1 for the distinction from depleted source stock.

after.prompt: Explain why groundwater is important for farming and settlement in the interior of Namibia.
after.canonical_answer: The interior has no perennial rivers, and its ephemeral rivers flow only for short periods after rain. Evaporation is very high, so open water in dams is lost quickly. Boreholes and wells reach aquifers that hold water all year and do not lose it to evaporation. This allows livestock farms and towns to have a supply in dry seasons and droughts.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor of no perennial rivers/ephemeral flow in the interior; 1 for the link to high evaporation from surface stores; 1 for boreholes tapping aquifers that store water all year; 1 for the effect of a dependable supply for farms and settlements.

before.prompt: Explain the error in placing the impounded reservoir south of a wall on a river flowing north to south. What direction test locates it?
before.canonical_answer: The confusion places stored upstream water downstream. Flow approaches the wall from the north, so the impounded reservoir backs into the northern upstream valley. Follow the incoming-flow direction to discriminate retained storage from released downstream water.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the upstream/downstream error; 1 for the correct north/upstream distinction and flow-direction test.

after.prompt: On a contour sketch, a river flows from north to south and a dam wall crosses it; the planned water level is the 255 m contour. A learner shades the reservoir south of the wall. Explain the error and the test that locates the reservoir correctly.
after.canonical_answer: The confusion places stored water downstream. Water approaching from the north is held back, so the correct reservoir lies north of the wall, filling the upstream valley up to the 255 m contour. The test is to follow the flow towards the wall and shade only the upstream valley below the stated water level.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the confusion of upstream with downstream; 1 for the correct distinction and discriminating test: shade the upstream (northern) valley up to the 255 m contour.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that Windhoek’s use of several water sources makes demand management unnecessary? The city’s documented approach combines surface supplies, groundwater and reclamation. Quantities, treatment, delivery and future inflows remain limited or variable; no unlimited reserve is stated. Judge dependable usable supply. [5]
before.canonical_answer: Disagree. A mix can diversify opportunities, but each source still has quantity, quality, operating and delivery conditions. Shared maintenance or energy constraints can also affect access. Demand management and loss reduction can help maintain useful service alongside supply measures. The existence of several sources does not establish that every future demand is met. A current judgement needs matched reserve, flow and demand records.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using the case evidence about its source mix, resource/service limits and the complementary role of demand or loss management.
1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting automatic adequacy from source count.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that Windhoek's water supply is now secure? Use Windhoek's sources and recent conditions in your answer. [5]
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. Windhoek uses several sources: the Von Bach, Swakoppoort and Omatako dams, its own boreholes and water reclaimed at Goreangab. After above-average rain in 2024/25 the city reported in August 2025 that reserves could last at least two rainy seasons, lifted water restrictions and began recharging its aquifer. However, Windhoek has no perennial river, evaporation from dams is very high, droughts recur, as in 2024, and the city's population keeps growing. Supply is secure for now, but only if the city keeps diversifying, recharging the aquifer and managing demand.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using evidence of the diverse sources, the August 2025 reserve position and aquifer recharge, weighed against no perennial river, high evaporation, recurring drought and rising demand.
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. partly agree: secure in the short term only with continued management.

after.text: China's one-child policy ran from about 1979-80 to 2015: most couples were limited to one child, couples who had extra children could be fined, and rural couples whose first child was a girl could often have a second. Its main demographic concerns were a male-biased sex ratio and rapid ageing. All couples could have two children from 1 January 2016, and on 31 May 2021 the leadership announced that couples could have a third child, with support measures set out in July 2021.

before: Namibia's 2023 census provides a dated source for studying uneven settlement. Its national total should not be spread uniformly across the land. Regional and local tables or maps show the actual variation. A national average can be useful for comparison while concealing large urban and rural differences. Use the correct administrative boundaries and date before combining population and area figures.
after: Namibia's 2023 census provides a dated source for studying uneven settlement. The national density was 3.7 people per km², but people are very unevenly spread. Khomas, which contains Windhoek, was the most populous region, with 494,605 people (16.4%), while Ohangwena (31.5 per km²) and Oshana (26.7 per km²) in the north were the most densely populated. //Kharas in the dry south was the most sparsely populated. Rainfall rises from almost nothing at the coast to over 600 mm a year in the far north-east, so the wetter north supports many farming villages; Windhoek attracts people with government and service jobs; and the coastal towns grow through ports, fishing and mining. Use the correct administrative boundaries and date before combining population and area figures.

before: Internal migration redistributes population and service needs. An urban destination can gain working-age residents and demand for housing, transport or schools. An origin can lose labour while receiving remittances or later return migrants with skills. The balance depends on who moves, duration, employment and ties. A larger urban population is therefore not automatically entirely caused by migration; births and deaths also contribute.
after: Internal migration redistributes population and service needs. An urban destination can gain working-age residents and demand for housing, transport or schools. An origin can lose labour while receiving remittances or later return migrants with skills. The balance depends on who moves, duration, employment and ties. Windhoek shows this. About 60% of its residents in 2001 and in 2011 were migrants not born in the city. Many, especially from the northern regions, settle in the northern and north-western parts of the city, mainly in informal settlements, where over 60% of the city's people live on 25% of its land. Khomas region grew from 342,141 people in 2011 to 494,605 in 2023, an increase of 44.6%, putting pressure on housing, water, sanitation and jobs.

before: Overpopulation refers to a situation where population pressure exceeds the support that the available resource and productive system can sustainably provide at the relevant living standard. Symptoms may include inadequate housing, jobs, water or services, but their causes also involve distribution, investment and management. A large population total alone cannot prove the condition. Identify the specific need, resource limit and access evidence.
after: Overpopulation refers to a situation where population pressure exceeds the support that the available resource and productive system can sustainably provide at the relevant living standard. Symptoms may include inadequate housing, jobs, water or services, but their causes also involve distribution, investment and management. A large population total alone cannot prove the condition. In Windhoek's crowded northern and north-western areas, for example, over 60% of the city's people live on a quarter of its land, and many lack adequate housing and services.

before: China provides a historical policy example that must be dated. The government's July 2021 account described a move to allow couples three children alongside measures intended to support births and respond to ageing. This contrasts with describing a restrictive one-child arrangement as today's unchanging policy. The source establishes the stated 2021 direction; it does not prove the later outcome or provide a current birth rate.
after: China is the best-known example of population control. From about 1979-80 to 2015 its one-child policy limited most couples to one child; couples who had extra children could be fined, although rural couples whose first child was a girl could often have a second. Births fell, but the policy contributed to a male-biased sex ratio and rapid ageing, leaving fewer young workers to support more older people. All couples were allowed two children from 1 January 2016, and on 31 May 2021 China announced that couples could have a third child, with support measures set out in July 2021 to encourage births.

before: Social and environmental influences on deaths include living conditions, food security, conflict, unsafe water, pollution and hazards. Their effects depend on exposure and response capacity. A flood can damage sanitation or services, while a prolonged food-access problem can weaken health. Population analysis should identify these routes rather than simply say the environment is poor. It should also avoid attributing an individual's illness or death without appropriate evidence.
after: Social and environmental influences on deaths include living conditions, food security, conflict, unsafe water, pollution and hazards. Their effects depend on exposure and response capacity. A flood can damage sanitation or services, while a prolonged food-access problem can weaken health. Disease can also change death rates sharply. Namibia was one of the five countries worst affected by HIV/AIDS: about one adult in five was living with HIV in 2004, and life expectancy at birth had fallen to 49 years by 2002, as many young adults died. Antiretroviral treatment, expanded from the mid-2000s, lets people with HIV live much longer.

before: Young dependants and older dependants commonly refer to age groups outside a chosen working-age band. In the standard teaching convention, young ages are under fifteen, older ages sixty-five or more and working ages fifteen to sixty-four. Use the bands actually stated in a resource. These are demographic categories, not a direct count of employed and unemployed people. Some working-age people do not earn, and some older people continue working or provide unpaid support.
after: Young dependants and older dependants commonly refer to age groups outside a chosen working-age band. In the standard teaching convention, young ages are under fifteen, older ages sixty-five or more and working ages fifteen to sixty-four. Use the bands actually stated in a resource. These are age categories. The economically active population is different: it is the people supplying labour, meaning those in work plus those unemployed but looking for and available for work. Some working-age people do not earn, and some older people continue working or provide unpaid support.

after: An assessment can test whether environmental conditions change alongside settlement growth. State the claim and choose relevant evidence, such as mapped land cover, water demand, waste collection or an environmental-quality score from a bi-polar survey. A bi-polar grid scores each site on pairs of opposite descriptions, such as no litter against much litter, on a scale such as -3 to +3, so that totals for a formal suburb and an informal settlement can be compared. after: If site observations are used, define a selection frame. Random, systematic and stratified sampling provide different rules for coverage and potential bias. before.prompt: Name the birth-policy direction announced by China in July 2021, when permission rose to three children.

marking_guidance: 1 mark for the relevant policy-direction point.

after.prompt: In 2021 China changed its birth policy so that couples could have more children than before. Name the number of children then allowed per couple.
after.canonical_answer: Three children.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the point: three children per couple.

before.prompt: Calculate the total age dependency ratio for 300 under fifteen, 600 aged fifteen–sixty-four and 100 sixty-five-plus.
before.canonical_answer: Dependants total 400; 400/600 is about 0.667, giving approximately 66.7 dependants per 100 working-age people.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the dependent-over-working-age method; 1 for the correct rounded answer 66.7; 1 for the ratio unit per 100 working-age people.

after.prompt: A population pyramid for Country X shows 140 people aged under 15 and 220 people aged 65 and over in every 1,000. Calculate the number of older people per young person, and use your answer to suggest the DTM stage the pyramid represents.
after.canonical_answer: 220 ÷ 140 = 1.57, so about 1.6 older people for every young person. More older than young people gives a narrow base and a wide top, which suggests stage 4 (or later), with low birth and death rates and long life expectancy.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the method (working): older ÷ young, 220 ÷ 140; 1 mark for the answer 1.6 (accept 1.57); 1 mark for stating it as a ratio of older people per young person and linking the top-heavy shape to stage 4 or later.

before.prompt: Explain the error in treating an ageing population’s problems as simply those of too many people overall. What test distinguishes them?
before.canonical_answer: The confusion substitutes total size for age composition. Ageing changes the older share and relevant care/support needs, while resource pressure from total size is a separate issue. Compare age bands and service needs alongside resources to discriminate the two.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the size/structure confusion; 1 for the correct distinction and discriminating age/service test.

after.prompt: Countries X and Y each have 1,000,000 people. In X, 40% are under 15 and 4% are 65 or over; in Y, 14% are under 15 and 26% are 65 or over. A learner says Y's problems are those of too many people. Explain the error and the test that distinguishes the two situations.
after.canonical_answer: The confusion treats total size as the cause, but X and Y have the same total, so size cannot explain Y's different problems. Y's problems come from its age structure: more pensions, health care and care for older people, with fewer young people entering work. The test is to compare the shares in each age group at equal totals rather than the total population.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the confusion of total population size with age structure (the totals are equal); 1 for the correct distinction (ageing problems such as pensions, health and care costs, a shrinking workforce) and the test of comparing age-group shares at equal totals.

before.prompt: Explain how a port or employment centre can support concentrated settlement despite a dry setting where usable water is supplied.
before.canonical_answer: Employment and trade create livelihood opportunities. Suitable water and infrastructure make settlement more feasible despite the physical constraint. People and services can concentrate around those opportunities, though actual growth needs population evidence.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for employment/trade as a factor; 1 for the livelihood link; 1 for the enabling water/infrastructure condition; 1 for the conditional concentration effect.

after.prompt: Explain why population density is high in the Ohangwena and Oshana regions of northern Namibia.
after.canonical_answer: Northern Namibia receives more rain than the dry south and west, because rainfall rises towards the north-east. This rain allows crops to be grown and livestock to be grazed, so many farming families can live on the land. Their homesteads and villages are close together, giving densities of 31.5 and 26.7 people per km², far above the national average of 3.7 per km².
marking_guidance: 1 mark for higher rainfall as a factor; 1 for the link to crop growing and grazing; 1 for many farming households living close together; 1 for the effect of high density, using census values or a comparison with the national average.

before.prompt: Explain how limited work at an origin and perceived jobs at a destination can encourage migration without proving every migrant gains work.
before.canonical_answer: The origin condition pushes departure while expected opportunities pull towards the destination. A residential move can follow, but employment depends on actual jobs, skills and access. The motive is not proof of the outcome.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for an origin factor; 1 for the push/pull link; 1 for the move mechanism; 1 for the conditional livelihood effect.

after.prompt: Explain why many people migrate from the northern regions of Namibia to Windhoek.
after.canonical_answer: In the rural north there are few paid jobs and farming depends on uncertain rainfall, which pushes people to leave. Windhoek pulls them with jobs, schools, health services and relatives who already live there. Many migrants settle in the northern and north-western parts of the city, often in informal settlements, so Khomas region grew by 44.6% between 2011 and 2023.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for a push factor at the origin (few jobs, rain-dependent farming); 1 for a pull factor link (jobs, services, relatives in Windhoek); 1 for the move and settlement in the northern/north-western areas or informal settlements; 1 for the effect of rapid growth of Windhoek/Khomas.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that China’s stated July 2021 move to allow three children with supporting measures proves births subsequently rose and ageing was resolved? The dated government account describes the policy direction and intended support, but this resource supplies no later fertility, age-structure or implementation results. Judge what the policy evidence establishes. [5]
before.canonical_answer: Disagree with the outcome claim. The dated account establishes an intended change and support direction, not measured later births or age structure. Costs, choices, access and delivery influence response, while ageing changes over a longer period. Implementation and suitable later demographic records are needed. The policy can have a relevant aim without proving its result or describing today’s complete arrangements.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using dated policy evidence, intention/outcome distinction, conditional response and timescale.
1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting demonstrated births/ageing outcomes from the announcement alone.

after.prompt: How far do you agree that China's one-child policy was a success? Use the policy's methods and results in your answer. [5]
after.canonical_answer: Partly agree. From about 1979-80 to 2015 most couples were limited to one child, with fines for extra births, and the birth rate fell, slowing China's population growth. However, the policy contributed to a male-biased sex ratio and to rapid ageing, so fewer young workers now support more older people. China allowed two children from 2016 and announced a three-child policy in 2021 to encourage births, which shows the government itself saw problems. The policy succeeded in slowing growth but created long-term problems.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judgement using evidence of the methods (one-child limit, fines, rural exception) and results: slower growth against the male-biased sex ratio, rapid ageing and the later two- and three-child changes.
1 C mark for a supported decision, e.g. partly agree: growth slowed but ageing and sex-ratio problems followed.

before.canonical_answer: Partly agree. before.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. About 90% of Namibians are Christian, so churches reach many people. They provide counselling, home visits and care for the sick, help orphans with food and school costs, and can reduce stigma and encourage testing; some faith-based institutions also provide treatment. However, churches cannot replace medical services, and some religious messages discourage condom use or present HIV as a moral failing, which can increase stigma. Their role is important mainly in care and support, alongside health services.

before: A veterinary cordon fence, the Red Line, separates the north from the centre and south. It began as a colonial boundary between 1896 and 1907 and became a physical fence in the early 1960s. It protects southern livestock from foot-and-mouth disease and lung sickness, so meat from the south can be exported and large commercial ranches developed there. Northern cattle must be quarantined before they can be moved south and cannot easily be exported, which raises costs and keeps most northern herds outside commercial production.

before.canonical_answer: Perennial rivers are concentrated near the national boundaries, while most interior channels flow only after rain. Named aquifers occur in several interior areas, so groundwater is important away from the perennial rivers. Interior dams also store surface water; the pattern does not mean all permanent water is at the border.

after.canonical_answer: Perennial rivers are concentrated near the national boundaries, while most interior channels flow only after rain.
